articles.title: Lula na Espanha: reunião com Sánchez encerra 1ª viagem pós-reeleição | G1
articles.standfirst: Presidente brasileiro foi à COP 31, na Turquia, e às Filipinas durante a cúpula de países do Sudeste Asiático para discutir minerais críticos
articles.summary: Lula na Espanha encerra seu primeiro giro internacional após reeleição, passando por Turquia e Filipinas para tratar de clima, defesa e minerais críticos.
articles.body:
O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) se reúne nesta segunda-feira (16) com o primeiro-ministro espanhol, Pedro Sánchez, em Madri, na Espanha.

Lula realiza sua primeira viagem internacional após ser reeleito para o quarto mandato presidencial. Na semana passada, o petista embarcou para a Turquia e depois seguiu para as Filipinas. A previsão é que o presidente embarque para Brasília ainda nesta segunda (16).

Em Madri, Lula realiza uma reunião restrita com o espanhol Pedro Sánchez no Palácio da Moncloa. Depois, o presidente participa de uma reunião ampliada e faz a foto oficial do encontro.

O primeiro-ministro espanhol participa das eleições no país, que estão previstas para o fim de novembro. Sánchez busca um apoio público de Lula e chegou a convidar o deputado André Janones (Rede-MG) para contribuir com sua campanha política.

Com uma comitiva que contou com Janones, Celso Amorim, assessor especial para assuntos internacionais, e ministros de seu governo , Lula fez sua primeira parada na Turquia para a COP 31, realizada na cidade turca de Antália.

➡️ COP se refere ao termo em inglês Conferece of Parties, ou Conferência das Partes. A cúpula é um evento anual que reúne representantes de diversos países, além de diplomatas, cientistas, sociedade civil e empresas privadas.

Antes da conferência do clima, teve reunião com o presidente turco, Recep Tayyip Erdogan. Segundo o governo brasileiro, os presidentes defenderam a ampliação do comércio entre os dois países e Lula destacou o interesse de estabelecer uma parceria "mais robusta na área de defesa" com a Turquia .

Já na COP, o presidente Lula cobrou que os países ricos cumpram os compromissos assumidos no enfrentamento às mudanças climáticas .

No primeiro discurso internacional após a reeleição , Lula mencionou que a crise climática também é marcada por desigualdades sociais e entre os países.

Na sequência, defendeu o princípio das “responsabilidades comuns, mas diferenciadas”, segundo o qual as nações desenvolvidas têm maior responsabilidade no enfrentamento da crise climática.

“Os países ricos se desenvolveram às custas do planeta e devem cumprir seus compromissos”, afirmou Lula.

Logo em seguida, no sábado (14), Lula seguiu para Manila, nas Filipinas, onde o petista se encontrou com o presidente filipino Ferdinand Marcos Jr. O presidente brasileiro defendeu que Brasil e Filipinas têm potencial para integrar cadeias produtivas nas áreas de minerais críticos, semicondutores e microeletrônica.

Segundo Lula, a ideia é aproximar centros de pesquisa, universidades e empresas dos países na área. O Brasil detém a segunda maior reserva global de terras raras. Já as Filipinas possuem um parque industrial voltado à montagem e produção de chips e componentes eletrônicos.

No domingo (15), Lula participou da 49ª cúpula da Associação de Nações do Sudeste Asiático (Asean). Na ocasião, o petista defendeu o aprofundamento das relações comerciais e diplomáticas com o bloco .

Lula afirmou que o Brasil está aberto a investimentos estrangeiros no setor de minerais críticos, mas que não permitirá a exploração desses recursos sem agregação de valor em território nacional.

O presidente também manifestou interesse em ampliar a cooperação com o bloco nas áreas de alta tecnologia, biocombustíveis, defesa e segurança alimentar.

Segundo Lula, o comércio entre o Brasil e os países da Asean movimentou US$ 38,4 bilhões em 2025, tornando o bloco o quinto maior parceiro comercial brasileiro.

DeSantis reacted to a Reuters report about the GOP resistance to an “appointment blitz.” “Ugh. And Republicans wonder why they have problems with base voter…
articles.body:
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) on Sunday knocked Republicans for pushing back on President Trump’s efforts to install more judges before Democrats take control in the 120th Congress in January.

DeSantis reacted to a Reuters report about the GOP resistance to an “appointment blitz.”

“Ugh. And Republicans wonder why they have problems with base voter enthusiasm,” DeSantis wrote Sunday on the social platform X .

The outlet reported that Republican lawmakers have confirmed 57 of Trump’s nominees for lifetime seats on district and appeals courts. Some Senate Republicans have blocked or questioned three nominees tapped for their home states.

The White House withdrew its nomination to place U.S. District Judge Lee Rudofsky to the 8th Circuit Court of Appeals after he was blocked by GOP Sens. John Boozman (Ark.) and Tom Cotton (Ark.). The administration swapped Rudofsky with Arkansas Supreme Court Justice J. ​Cody Hiland.

Other Republicans set to leave the Senate in January, namely Sens. Alan Armstrong (Okla.), John Cornyn (Texas) and Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) –– the latter two being on the Senate Judiciary Committee –– have either withheld support or helped block candidates.

Tillis also said there must be more “respect” from the White House to senators when tapping judges for their states, the report stated.

A White House official told Reuters that they “expect all judicial nominees pending in the Senate to be confirmed this year.”

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) told the outlet last week that judicial confirmations were a top priority, with 23 judicial nominations still pending. Tillis and Cornyn have indicated a willingness to block some of these nominees.

“What we need to do is make sure that every nominee for a lifetime judgeship, either on the federal district court, or more importantly, even the circuit courts of appeals, we need to get them confirmed,” Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) said in an interview with “ The Cats Roundtable with John Catsimatidis ” on Sunday.

Cramer told the host that after the Senate’s vote to confirm judicial nominee Gregory Carl Cook to serve on a U.S. district court in Alabama on Thursday, the Senate could “take up another batch of judges” this week, adding that it was a priority “as conservatives” and “Donald Trump’s top priority.”

articles.title: After a nationwide ground stop, US faces aviation infrastructure questions
articles.summary: Trump has requested $50bn for upgrades, but Democratic lawmakers are asking for transparency before spending more.
articles.body:
Last Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) grounded all flights in the United States for nearly four hours due to a reported equipment failure.

It was only the second time since the attacks on September 11, 2001, that such an order was given.

More than 9,000 flights were cancelled, and an estimated 1.5 million passengers were left stranded.

Officials blamed the disruptions on an upgrade gone awry. The routers used to communicate with aeroplanes in mid-flight had suddenly stopped working , and pilots were no longer able to speak on their usual frequencies.

As of Sunday, officials were still working to return the system to normal. “As we look to the end of the day and into tomorrow, we should be running at full capacity,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told CBS News, while acknowledging continued delays.

But the situation has led to scrutiny over whether the nationwide ground-stop could have been prevented.

While President Donald Trump has blamed a lack of funding from Congress, critics say billions of dollars have already been allocated for badly needed upgrades. The work, they say, is what has lagged behind.

Democratic lawmakers have also questioned the Trump administration’s choice of contractors to install the upgrades.

“Secretary Duffy and the Federal Aviation Administration have received historical and monumental investments over the last two years,” Democratic Representative Rosa DeLauro said in a statement on Sunday.

“Congress has shown its willingness to modernize the FAA’s systems and support its workforce as part of annual bipartisan legislation, but we need a competent partner at the Department of Transportation to carry this out in a sustainable, transparent manner.”

Duffy has indicated that investigations are ongoing into what caused the malfunction on Friday.

But he has described the problem as starting at “a remote FAA location” where workers from the defence contractor L3Harris were replacing ageing copper wire with fibre optic lines.

A router used for communication reportedly began to malfunction, sending out 1,000 attempts to log onto the FAA’s system every four or five seconds, overloading the entire network.

In an interview on Sunday with NBC’s Meet the Press, Duffy stopped short of blaming L3Harris.

“Was this a faulty installation by L3Harris that was doing the work for us? Was it a fault of the router itself? We have to do that investigation and make sure we take precautions,” he said.

Though Duffy did suggest he preferred to part ways with the company, which owns a significant chunk of the FAA’s telecommunications infrastructure.

“I want to get away from L3Harris and get to a new one, but they own the network,” Duffy told Meet the Press. “I can’t cancel the network that they own, and I operate on.”

L3Harris has existed since 2019, following a merger between the Harris Corporation and L3 Technologies.

It is one of the largest defence contractors in the country, and its involvement with the FAA’s telecommunications network stretches back to 2002, when the Harris Corporation was awarded a billion-dollar contract to modernise the network’s systems.

But Friday’s mass grounding was not the first time L3Harris’s systems were involved in flight delays and problems with communications during an upgrade operation.

In November 2009, for example, the FAA’s network experienced a smaller outage as upgrades were being made to a router in Los Angeles, according to an agency investigation .

“The most notable impact to the flying public was the inability of the FAA to process electronic flight plan data,” a report explained.

“As a result, these flight plans had to be entered into the FAA air traffic control systems manually, causing the delay of over 800 flights that morning.”

In a statement after Friday’s grounding, L3Harris said it was supporting the FAA’s current probe and had already replaced 70 percent of the system’s copper wire with fibre optics.

“L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously,” it said.

Critics point out that many of the problems associated with the FAA’s telecommunications systems predate L3Harris’s involvement and stem from ageing infrastructure.

The FAA has aimed for years to replace some 5,170 lengths of copper wiring dating to the 1960s, which is used by routers and other communication gear.

Ageing copper, however, is just one of the tech problems the FAA faces.

In a September report, the Government Accountability Office, an independent agency tasked with reviewing government departments, highlighted a series of areas in dire need of upgrades.

Computers used by air traffic controllers to display key information like flight approach paths and aviation warnings were using obsolete hardware, including screens from the 1980s and floppy disk drives.

Thousands of radios and specialised switches that allow radio communication over phone lines also rely on obsolete technology that is no longer manufactured.

The agency had been forced to look for replacement parts on the online marketplace eBay, according to Duffy.

The Government Accountability Office also pointed to the continued use of paper flight strips, slips of paper printed for each flight coming into an air traffic controller’s area of responsibility.

Those documents help decide how to coordinate movements like takeoffs and landings so planes do not collide. But the print-out system has already caused dangerous situations.

In August 2023, for instance, a printer used to print flight strips at San Diego International airport jammed. As air traffic controllers tried to fix it, a Southwest Airlines aircraft almost hit a Cessna jet by about 30 metres (100 feet).

Before Friday’s incident, the last national ground stop happened in January 2023, after the FAA’s Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) system stopped working.

Built in 1985, the NOTAM system was responsible for sending emergency messages out about dangerous weather, congestion or other safety issues.

Its failure prompted the FAA to undertake a major review. The Government Accountability Office ultimately found that, out of the 138 systems the FAA relied on, 51 were unsustainable, and another 54 were potentially unsustainable because of ageing technology.

Fifty-eight of those systems, according to the accountability office, had a critical impact on the safety of air traffic in the US.

In September, the Government Accountability Office reported that the FAA had failed to meet at least four of its 11 recommendations for modernising air traffic systems.

One reason for the failure was the complexity of the upgrades. The FAA reportedly has 11,389 individual upgrade projects on its agenda, and it has struggled to coordinate the repairs, leaving it unable to prepare for network-wide problems.

The accountability office also determined that the FAA failed to make upgrades because it was not properly overseeing work done by its contractors.

It also pointed to a lack of funding. Unlike many critical government agencies, the FAA’s budget is not mandated by law, so Congress has to approve spending for the agency each year.

Even if Congress does allocate funding, the Trump administration does not have to use all of the money right away, and Democrats have pointed to unspent funds as part of the problem.

Though Congress allocated $12.5bn for the FAA’s upgrades in 2025, the Trump administration has only committed to spending $4bn of that sum. Only approximately $1bn has been spent so far.

Still, Duffy has argued that the FAA needs at least $50bn in the wake of Friday’s grounding.

Democrats like DeLauro have called that sum a “ransom without a real plan to deliver”. She urged full transparency from Duffy and the FAA.

“No federal leader should be free to do their work without Congressional oversight,” she said.

articles.title: Moore on the chances of a 2028 presidential bid: ‘I’m still sorting it out’
articles.summary: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) on Sunday said he was still deliberating on the decision to go from the governor’s mansion to the White House with a 2028 presidential run but noted that he was “still sorting” out that decision. Independent journalist Chuck Todd asked Moore in an interview on Noosphere if he was still…
articles.body:
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) on Sunday said he was still deliberating on the decision to go from the governor’s mansion to the White House with a 2028 presidential run but noted that he was “still sorting” out that decision.

Independent journalist Chuck Todd asked Moore in an interview on Noosphere if he was still thinking about a possible run after winning a second term earlier this month, having already said he would serve a full term as governor. Todd said he read that as “more ambiguous than others did” and asked if he was correct or not.

Moore praised his work while leading Maryland, saying the state’s progress has humbled him and that its “performance is justified as being part of this conversation.”

“But the honest answer is, I don’t know,” he said. “I’m still sorting it out.”

Todd later said that there are “a lot of people” who “assume that this decision’s already made” and that the governor was “just waiting for the right time.”

“Well, I’ll put it this way,” Moore answered. “Five years ago was when I first started thinking about running for governor, running for any office. And when people are like, ‘You really never thought about?’ sometimes I think to myself, ‘I’m a kid who at 11 years old had handcuffs on my wrists. I was raised by an immigrant single mother. She didn’t get her first job that gave her benefits after my dad died until I was 14 years old.”

He later repeated that he did not know, later saying that there was still work to be done in Maryland, “and I’m proud of our progress, but progress is not mission completion.”

Moore previously did not give a clear answer to The Baltimore Banner during an interview in October when asked if he would see through the entire duration of a second term if he defeated Republican Dan Cox at the polls. He said he would not have ran for reelection “if I was not committed to the people of Maryland.”

He twice said in 2025 that he was not running for president, telling NBC News’s Kristen Welker that he would serve a full term when asked if he ruled out a presidential run and telling “The View” co-host Joy Behar that he was not running .

“Wait a minute, what if we really, really, really need you, though?” Behar asked to laughter.

Moore’s national profile has been on the rise amid his criticisms of President Trump, particularly after the president threatened to deploy the National Guard to Baltimore.

Other Democrats with rising national profiles who have taken Trump to task have also been seen as potential 2028 Democratic presidential contenders.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) has been an outspoken critic, at times lampooning Trump on social media and clashing with him over his deployments of the National Guard and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to Los Angeles in June 2025.

Newsom told the Turkish state-run news outlet Anadolu Agency that he will decide on a run for president in January.

“I’ll make the determination at the beginning of the year, so we’ll spend the next few weeks with the family and make a decision early January,” he told the outlet while attending the COP31 climate summit last Thursday.

Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday blasted “incoming freshmen” Democrats elected following the 2026 midterm elections for “acting like prosecutors” in joining lawmakers’ calls to open investigations into President Trump and his administration.

Fox News host Mark Levin asked Blanche on his show “ Life, Liberty & Levin ” if Congress can act “like a judiciary and an executive prosecutorial operation.”

“No, that’s exactly right,” Blanche answered. “And what you’ve heard, these incoming freshmen, and some of them are brand new to Congress –– so hopefully they’ll learn –– is they’re acting like prosecutors. They’re acting like they’re going to cut subpoenas left and right, and they’re going to investigate, and they’re going to have a trial and a conviction, and that’s absolutely not their job.”

Blanche said Democrats can conduct oversight, “but that’s not the rhetoric we’re hearing right now from these guys,” later adding that he hopes it’s only rhetoric and that they will “actually try to do their job, try to work with President Trump. Like he said, he would work with them.”

But should Democrats open investigations, “we’re going to be there and we’re not going to just stand by willingly and let them destroy their function and we’re not going to let that happen.”

“They said ‘lawyer up,'” Blanche said, referring to remarks made by incoming House Oversight Committee Chair Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) shortly after the midterms. “You only lawyer up if you’re concerned there’s going to be some kind of criminal investigation.”

Blanche also referred to comments Garcia made last week saying that White House chief of staff Stephen Miller “should be preserving documents” before the new Congress starts.

“They went after the chief of staff for the President of the United States without saying anything he did wrong,” the attorney general noted. “Because he’s done nothing wrong except to work hard for the American people, work hard for President Trump.”

“And again, I have –– I really have hope this rhetoric stops, but unfortunately, I’m not optimistic given what they’ve said in the past two weeks, but maybe they’ll change their tune before January,” Blanche continued.

Garcia’s comment reverberated among other Democratic lawmakers calling to investigate alleged corruption, as well as continue probes into Trump’s ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and the activities carried out by the now-defunct Department of Government Efficiency at the start of Trump’s second term.

White House special counsel Will Scharf clapped back at Garcia last week, writing in a letter that the administration will consider whether the investigations and subsequent subpoenas could amount to criminal activity .

“We’re going to see what happens in January, but we’re ready to fight tooth and nail here if that’s the road they want to go down,” Scharf later said on Newsmax.

Some Democratic lawmakers responded saying the administration was hiding things revolving the president in connection with their vows to conduct oversight. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) said Scharf’s reply to Garcia was “an act of desperation” and that Democratic lawmakers “should not be afraid of them.”

Other Democrats were defiant, with Rep. Stephen Lynch (D-Mass.) responding, “ Come at me, bro .”

articles.title: U.S. attorney warns Sen. Elizabeth Warren against investigating Trump associates
articles.summary: A Justice Department official on Sunday accused Sen.
articles.body: A Justice Department official on Sunday accused Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., of intending to target private individuals close to President Donald Trump with investigations. The allegation came in a letter similar to others sent to congressional Democrats. U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas Aaron Reitz sent a letter to Warren — who is likely the incoming chairwoman of the Senate Banking Committee — calling on her to preserve documents related to investigations of Trump allies. Reitz noted that Warren appears “eager to wield your future gavel like a tomahawk, hunting for the scalps of President Trump’s private associates.” Reitz referenced a Nov. 11 letter in which Warren, Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., and Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., asked Meredith O’Rourke, a National Park Foundation board member and top fundraiser for Trump, to retain documents related to funding for the White House ballroom and other projects. Reitz accused the three lawmakers of “demanding sweeping information about her and other private citizens and entities who associate with President Trump.” The letter to Warren signals an expansion of Reitz’s inquiry into congressional Democrats tasked with government oversight. When Democrats take control of Congress next year, Garcia is likely to take the gavel of the House Oversight Committee, while Blumenthal is expected to lead the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs’ Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations. Last week, the White House issued a threat to congressional Democrats against probes into the administration. Since their midterm victories, Democrats have said Trump family businesses and immigration enforcement are some of their top targets for investigation. Reitz’s letter referenced an op-ed from Warren earlier this month in Time magazine, in which the senator wrote, “With astonishing brazenness, Trump has attempted to reengineer the federal government into a corruption machine designed to rake in profits for himself, his family, and his cronies.” Reitz also accused Warren of planning to target businesses that associate with Trump, referencing an appearance on CBS’ “Face the Nation” in which Warren said tech CEOs, Wall Street executives and giant corporations who have broken the law “better get ready for some investigations — serious ones.” “The context sends a strong smoke signal: you intend to target private individuals close to President Trump,” Reitz said. A spokesperson for Warren did not immediately respond to a request for comment Sunday night. Reitz, a former chief of staff to Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, has sent similar letters to Blumenthal and Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., warning them against investigating Trump associates and calling on them to preserve documents. Reitz posted his letter to Warren on X, and Trump reposted it to Truth Social later Sunday. The letter to Warren also contained numerous references to Native Americans, such as “scalps,” “war cries” and “tomahawk,” a dig at Warren over her past claims of Native American descent.

articles.title: Why did Republicans lose? Don’t accept Team Trump’s excuses.
articles.summary: Voters are really angry about Trump. It’s no more complicated than that.
articles.body:
Republicans suffered a major beating last week in the 2026 midterms. For this, the right can thank the Trump White House, whose approval rating has been underwater consistently since its tariff “Liberation Day” in April 2025 .

It should come as no surprise that Republicans took a walloping in a cycle where many of its candidates were as unqualified as they were unlikeable — and where many of them were handpicked by a president about as popular as late-stage cancer.

A smarter party would next time nominate candidates whose entire pitch is not simply “The president said I could.”

But try telling that to the hangers-on of the MAGA movement, some of whom insist the problem was that the Republican Party did not MAGA hard enough. Heritage Foundation President Kevin Roberts, for example, believes the takeaway from last week is not that Republicans should broaden their appeal or rein in the party’s fringes, but that they were too moderate, too soft.

Roberts took exception to Republican Sen. John Thune’s (R-S.D.) remarks last week on Fox News.

“We’ve got to start talking to independent voters,” Thune said. “It’s a third of the electorate, and they went against us in four of the top Senate races in the country. We lost them by over 30 points. You cannot make that up with just Republican votes. You’ve got to be able to talk to the people out there who in general elections are going to decide it. And largely, that’s going to be an economic message. And so, we’ve got to get back to basics.”

In Roberts’s view, “‘We’ve got to start talking to independent voters’ is Swamp talk for ‘run to the middle.’” The Heritage president added: “Running to the middle is not what got Trump popularly elected in 2024, but it is what got Republicans crushed in the midterms. Bold conservatism is what will attract independent voters and win elections.”

Which raises the question: In exactly what sense did Republicans run to the middle? Are we to believe that last week’s results are unconnected to the deeply unpopular White House’s direct involvement in several key races? Are we supposed to buy that the electoral drubbing had nothing to do with the administration’s disastrously unpopular style of governance or the poor quality of a mostly MAGA-approved slate of candidates?

Nominating the scandal-plagued Ken Paxton in Texas and Lindsey Graham’s little sister in South Carolina — both handpicked by Trump over the vocal objections of prominent state officials and local party leaders — was “running to the middle?” Anointing Vivek Ramaswamy for governor of Ohio — again against the judgment of successful state Republican officials — was “running to the middle?”

Maybe the midterm results are a response to the White House’s make-it-up-as-we-go approach to governance. They are possibly even a response to the White House’s flagrant acts of corruption, including many dubious cryptocurrency schemes and Trump’s hilariously shameless promise to cut voters $5,000 checks if Republicans won.

Speaking of self-dealing on the taxpayer’s dime, where, exactly, does Heritage place the White House’s protectionist tariffs on the scale of “bold conservatism?”

No, “running to the middle” was not the problem. The problem was a slate of crummy candidates and their marriage to a president whose second term is best described as Versailles Part Two — an operation devoted almost entirely to self-enrichment, punctuated by multiple acts of frivolous self-indulgence, and staffed by a revolving door of cranks , incompetents , and unabashed opportunists .

Darline Graham did not lose in South Carolina because she “ran to the middle.” She lost because she was an obviously unqualified candidate. But she was uplifted by an unpopular president and thus received her nomination.

Is the new electoral map the fault of the middle? Or does it have something to do with Republican obeisance to a White House best known for a poorly executed war, high costs of living, inflation, tariffs, chaotic and lethal ICE raids on public streets, self-enrichment schemes from current and former staff and a bevy of expensive, self-aggrandizing projects — arches, reflecting pools, demolitions, ballrooms, and fights over renaming the Kennedy Center?

When such an administration is at the forefront of an election cycle, do not be surprised when average voters go the other way.

No wonder Democrats flipped eight or nine Senate seats. No wonder not a single Democratic incumbent lost.

Roberts can complain all he wants about a “moderate” bogeyman. But before Trump, Republicans still knew how to win Senate seats in Iowa, Kansas and North Carolina. The old Republican Party was at least competitive in Arizona and Georgia, and it clearly dominated in Texas, which just went blue across the board.

As for actual conservatism — as opposed to whatever it is the White House and Heritage are hawking these days — the midterms were not a complete disaster. Conservatives can take pride in the passage of statewide ballot measures limiting the power of government, requiring voter ID and barring males from playing in women’s and girls’ sports.

The story of the 2026 midterms is clear for anyone honest enough to admit it: Voters are really angry about Trump. It’s no more complicated than that, even though the MAGA hangers-on will insist otherwise.

Becket Adams is a journalist and media critic in Washington.

articles.title: Duffy plays damage control after FAA outage
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ FAA blame game ▪ Lutnick under fire ▪ Van Hollen brushes off doubts ▪ Peltola getting closer Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy conducted a media blitz Sunday morning when he appeared on all five main political talk shows to address the concerns and backlash facing the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) following its…
articles.body:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy conducted a media blitz Sunday morning when he appeared on all five main political talk shows to address the concerns and backlash facing the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) following its nationwide outage.

Completing what’s known as a “full Ginsburg,” named after Monica Lewinsky ‘s lawyer William Ginsburg , Duffy pointed the finger at past administrations and Congress for not providing the FAA with additional funding to prevent the type of crisis that happened Friday. He reiterated his push for lawmakers to approve an additional $50 billion for the agency to modernize the air traffic control system.

“When we do work and things go wrong, of course I’m the secretary. But I also have to acknowledge what was delivered to me,” Duffy said on CNN. “I have systems that are from the ’90s. I have radar that are from the ’60s and ’70s.”

The impacts of the national ground stop, which lasted for several hours before it was lifted Friday evening, are still being felt days later. More than 10,000 flights within, into or out of the United States were delayed Sunday, and more than 2,300 were canceled, according to the flight-tracking website FlightAware .

The last nationwide ground stop was issued in 2023 for about 90 minutes when an outage occurred with the pilot notification system from a contractor. The last time before that was Sept. 11, 2001.

This time, Trump administration officials said “incredibly old” air traffic control systems are responsible. Duffy said at a press conference Saturday that a contractor called L3Harris had been replacing an old copper wire with a new fiber cable when the outage occurred. He said the FAA is still investigating the exact cause.

Duffy and other officials similarly advocated for greater funding to modernize the air traffic control system last year in the aftermath of the deadly January 2025 midair collision between an Army helicopter and passenger plane that claimed more than 60 lives at Reagan Washington National Airport.

In September, Duffy asked Congress for $30 billion in funding for new technology, control towers and airport improvements across the country. Now, he’s upping that number to $50 billion.

“Let’s finish this job: new hardware, new software, new telecommunication,” he said during a briefing Friday night.

Duffy argued Sunday that the $12.5 billion Congress had previously approved for air traffic control upgrades , as part of the “One Big, Beautiful Bill,” is “not nearly enough” to fix the problems facing the system after “decades of lack of investment.”

The push is being met with a mixed reaction in Congress.

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said no investigation is needed into the FAA’s ground stop and instead the focus should be on further investment . He vowed that lawmakers would work to “get it done.”

Rep. Tim Burchett (R-Tenn.) on Saturday called for his party’s leaders in Congress to move quickly but expressed some doubt about the ability of additional funding to get through the Senate.

“Both Speaker Johnson and [Senate Majority] Leader [John] Thune (R-S.D.) need to step up to the daggum plate … and pass a clean bill,” he said.

Burchett pointed to the Airspace Location and Enhanced Risk Transparency (ALERT) Act, which was introduced in the aftermath of the 2025 crash to improve collision prevention technologies. The bill passed the House in April but hasn’t received a vote in the Senate.

Democrats said they would support additional funding for the FAA if it would help but pushed back on Duffy’s argument that Congress is responsible for the current situation.

“It’s really rich to hear the secretary pointing the fingers at Congress when Congress has given the administration what they asked for,” Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) said Sunday. “If they need more, they should come up and justify it. I will support what is necessary to have a safe system and a reliable system.”

President Trump blamed former President Biden ‘s administration in Truth Social posts on Sunday, urging Congress to approve funding for a new air traffic control system.

“We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs. Congress must approve,” he said, adding that the Biden administration “set it back years.”

Rep.-elect Dan Koh (D-Mass.) accused Trump of rewriting history.

“President Biden had historic funding, not only to the FAA, but over a trillion dollars’ worth of infrastructure money, a lot of it that Donald Trump has reversed on the grounds of it being too woke,” Koh said Sunday during an appearance on MS NOW.

The Democratic ranking members of the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure and the aviation subcommittee said in a joint statement that only $1 billion of the $12.5 billion has been spent so far, and only $4.3 billion has been obligated for a specific purpose.

“Explain to Congress, again, why they need more money?” the lawmakers said.

Duffy said during his appearance on Fox News that the approved funding will be all deployed by the end of 2028.

“But I have no money for a new network. I don’t have any new money to build new software to separate planes in the airspace.”

▪ The Hill : Duffy says he can’t cancel contract with firm behind outage.

▪ The Hill : Security breaches, tarmac collision exacerbate aftermath.

Trump said the Interior Department will appeal a ruling from a federal judge preventing the administration from closing East Potomac Park to construct a championship-length golf course that he has planned. The decision delays any closure for at least two more weeks.

Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) said he’s not sure whether Heidi Overton will receive enough support for her nomination to become Food and Drug Administration head to advance past the Senate Health Committee, which he chairs. The vote is scheduled for Wednesday.

A federal prosecutor warned Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) of potential legal consequences of her plans to investigate the president and his allies. U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz demanded that Warren preserve documents related to her upcoming oversight efforts. The demand follows similar warnings Reitz made to Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) and Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.).

U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Maryland, speaks during a Democratic conference Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, in Denver. (AP Photo/David Zalubowski)

CHECKING THE LIST : Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) projected confidence in his bid to become Senate majority leader against Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) on Sunday, rejecting the idea that he can’t win as a “bunch of nonsense.”

The Hill’s Alexander Bolton reported that Schumer’s allies are predicting he will receive more than 40 votes, the overwhelming majority of the Democratic Caucus, in the leadership contest against Van Hollen, slamming the challenge as a “distraction.”

But Van Hollen said Sunday on CNN that several senators included on the list have privately told him that they would support his challenge.

“I can tell you that a number of those people on that list have actually committed to voting for me, and the others are very open to the idea of change,” he said.

Schumer has received public backing from more than a dozen senators, while Van Hollen has received endorsements from four current or incoming senators.

▪ The Hill : Van Hollen calls to abolish filibuster, rules out 2028 run.

▪ The Hill : John Fetterman says Van Hollen as leader would be ‘troubling.’

IN THE CROSSHAIRS : Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has found himself taking fire from critics, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent , over his approach to controls on AI chip exports amid the scandal surrounding Nvidia.

Reports have indicated Lutnick has taken a softer approach to Nvidia’s AI chip sales to China and failed to put the Singaporean company Megaspeed on the trade entity blacklist. Jensen Huang , Nvidia’s CEO until he resigned on Thursday, had been having an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang .

U.S. intelligence believes that Alice Huang was a spy for China.

Van Hollen on Sunday called on Lutnick to be fired.

The commerce secretary has agreed to testify before Congress following bipartisan calls for him to appear, but Bessent has emerged as a chief critic of Lutnick’s conduct.

“Treasury, War, USTR [U.S. Trade Representative] and State … were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months,” he said Friday during an interview on CNBC’s “Squawk Box.”

The Hill’s Miranda Nazzaro and Max Rego report on how the blame game is starting within the Trump administration.

▪ The Hill : Nvidia scandals throw wrench into Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping .

▪ The Hill : GOP House member says blaming Lutnick is ‘premature.’

▪ The New York Times : Lutnick pushed to weaken chip rules that overlap with family business.

INCHING CLOSER : Democrat Mary Peltola ticked toward the coveted majority of the vote in her Senate race against incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) as she tries to secure enough votes to avoid a ranked choice tabulation.

The most recent tally of votes shows Peltola leading by more than 10,000 votes, equal to almost 4 points. She currently has 49.94 percent of the counted votes to Sullivan’s 45.96 percent, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Peltola seems to be in an increasingly strong position to win the seat, but she’s still just short of the 50 percent she needs to win outright. Few ballots remain to be counted, but they all must be tallied by Wednesday.

The president will travel to Anchorage, Alaska, en route to Manila, Philippines, to participate in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit.

Vice President Vance speaks at the 2nd Marine Aircraft Wing’s annual Marine Corps Birthday Ball in New Bern, N.C., on Nov. 12, 2026. (AP Photo/Matt Rourke)

IN OR OUT : Republicans are discussing the wisdom of candidates sitting out the 2028 presidential race to wait for 2032 in the aftermath of the GOP’s brutal losses in the midterms.

The Hill’s Amie Parnes reports that the party’s performance and concerns about Trump’s record-low approval ratings are factoring into the decisions of some possible Republican presidential contenders.

“How can a candidate run in 2028 when they have to criticize the policies of a sitting president with a large amount of sway with the Republican base?” said one GOP operative who is close to a lawmaker weighing a future presidential bid. “It’s a suicide mission.”

Vice President Vance has been viewed as the front-runner for the 2028 GOP nomination, but Parnes reports that his allies have quietly wondered if this is the right time.

CNN reported Friday that Vance has given serious consideration to not running in 2028. The outlet reported that Vance hasn’t made up his mind yet, but those in his orbit said he’s thinking simultaneously about the future of the MAGA movement and his family.

Parnes notes that the political winds could change, just as Democrats were depressed and Republicans were feeling bullish after the 2024 election. Republican strategists said the party won’t be conceding the next election and will pour resources into the battle.

They’re hoping Democrats will overreach with their new majorities in Congress and damage their own brand.

▪ The Hill : Democrats bullish on the south after midterm gains.

Container ships are seen through haze in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran, on Nov. 14, 2026. (Amirhosein Khorgooi, ISNA via AP)

STANDING IN THE WAY : Bahrain said it intercepted multiple Iranian drones during an attack that Tehran directed at U.S. bases in the Gulf nation.

The strikes mark the first interceptions of Iranian drone attacks by Bahrain since September. The Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said the attacks were retaliation for “hostile U.S. actions.”

The U.S. and Iran have traded some strikes in recent weeks despite a relative calm period in the conflict as Trump weighs whether to renew fresh attacks against the regime.

The U.S. military struck radar detectors and missile launchers on Iran’s Qeshm Island earlier this month, just a day before the midterms, that officials said were defensive in nature for Iran “using surface-to-air missiles against U.S. assets.”

The IRGC claimed Friday that it struck an early-warning radar facility in Bahrain, but the U.S. denied this, saying it intercepted two drones.

Trump has recently suggested he may hold off on additional strikes against Iran as long as peace talks continue in a positive direction. He said last week that the war is “effectively over” and the U.S. has won.

But The Hill’s Ellen Mitchell reports that the conflict is still costing the U.S. billions of dollars to keep U.S. forces at the ready abroad.

▪ The Hill : Israeli strike in Gaza kills senior Hamas commander.

Could Trump turn against the AI barons? William Liang writes in The Hill.

Republicans must embrace early voting to win again , Andrew Follett writes in The Hill.

Referee Don Willard officiates during the first half of an NFL football game between the Indianapolis Colts and the Miami Dolphins on Nov. 15, 2026, in Indianapolis. (AP Photo/ Jeff Roberson)

And finally … The FAA ground stop caused NFL referee Don Willard to possibly make history as he worked two games in one day.

The NFL said the impact on national air travel caused it to adjust officiating assignments for the week and reassign officials to games within driving distance of their hometown. That resulted in Willard, a side judge, being assigned to both the 1 p.m. game between the Miami Dolphins and Indianapolis Colts (in Indiana) and the “Sunday Night Football” game between the Pittsburgh Steelers and Cincinnati Bengals (in Ohio).

The NFL Referees Association told NBC News that to the best of its knowledge, this is the first time an official has worked two games in one day. The ground stop also had significant implications for college football this weekend, as teams were stranded ahead of traveling for Saturday’s games.

articles.title: Voters spoke clearly about biological reality. Will leaders listen?
articles.summary: Voters delivered more than one message last Tuesday.
articles.body:
Voters were not subtle last Tuesday. They rejected the current direction of the country. But gas and groceries weren’t the only things on their minds. They also delivered a clear message on biological reality.

In the months ahead, both parties will study what worked and what did not. Here’s what’s already clear: We cannot fight for truth without practicing and modeling it. Too many candidates and politicians on both sides of the aisle have fallen woefully short. Americans are hungry for leadership that models integrity, competence, and principle, and for platforms built on truth and human flourishing — ideas that transcend political labels.

The clearest proof is the success of state ballot measures protecting girls’ sports and spaces.

Arizona voters passed a measure that builds on existing state law keeping women’s sports for women. It extends those protections to women’s private spaces, athletic associations, and private schools, and it defines “sex” by an individual’s original birth certificate.

Nebraska voters wrote their 2025 law into their state constitution. It requires K-12 and higher education schools to designate teams as male, female, or co-ed, and it keeps women’s sports free from men claiming a female identity.

You might expect that from Nebraska or even Arizona — but then came Colorado and Washington. In Colorado, a measure that protects girls’ sports passed, and another that protects children from dangerous transition surgeries.

Closest to my heart is my home state of Washington, where voters went to the ballot box to say — by double digits — that girls deserve fairness, safety, and privacy, no matter their zip code. That is huge in a state that has made women’s sports headlines all year. At a Seattle Storm WNBA game , the team’s co-owner spewed obscenities at young girls wearing XX-XY Athletics shirts in support of the ballot measure and Sophie Cunningham’s call for safety for women and girls.

In Puyallup, Washington, state and school officials allowed a male wrestler to compete against then-15-year-old wrestler Kallie Keeler , which resulted in serious harm. Her emergency petition is pending before the U.S. Supreme Court. And in Camas, a male athlete who switched to the girls’ cross country team midyear took the final qualifying spot from a deserving young woman from Puyallup High School and competed in the women’s state finals this month.

Despite these harms, many elected officials in Washington and Colorado have criticized these measures. Never mind that the voters who elected them are the same ones who adopted the measures. And now, the American Civil Liberties Union has asked a Washington judge to undo the people’s vote and strip away protections for girls.

But the ACLU can’t erase truth or change biology. Alliance Defending Freedom filed a motion to intervene to defend Washington’s new law on behalf of young female athletes.

Our daughters have been told to sit on the sidelines as spectators in their own sports for far too long. Washington voters saw them and crossed political lines to take a stand for truth, and their will should be respected.

Pundits will dissect this election for months. But some things, like truth, don’t change and can’t be erased. Truth can only be rediscovered or rejected. That includes the truths that men and women are different; that we can neither choose nor change our sex; and that our daughters deserve fairness, privacy, and safety. These truths are worth defending. They always will be.

Voters protected them on Nov. 3. We will defend them. But the fact that activists like the ACLU still think our daughters should sit this one out reveals there is still much more work to do, and that work is up to us, the people..

America was founded on self-evident truths: that we are each created equal and possess God-given rights, including the right to live and speak the truth. On those truths, our founders built the most prosperous and free nation in history. But it is our responsibility to keep those truths self-evident for the next generation — to cultivate, elect, and hold accountable leaders who will both listen to and uphold truth.

To the leaders whom voters just chose: Truth isn’t partisan. Lies always leave behind victims. And a free people cannot remain free without truth. Embrace the truth that leads to human flourishing, or voters will find leaders who will.

Kristen Waggoner is CEO, president, and chief counsel of Alliance Defending Freedom .

articles.title: Beneath the blue wave is a moral earthquake
articles.summary: Trump does not grasp the concept of public service. He treats the job as if he were CEO of the world’s largest for-profit corporation, benefiting from an utterly passive board of directors. That’s about to change.
articles.body:
A tsunami is an awesome force of nature, but the big waves are caused by something deeper. Most tsunamis result from underwater earthquakes . That may be what we saw in the midterm election.

Although the big blue wave was a political realignment, it might have signaled a deeper moral realignment — a tectonic shift in which the electorate has demanded honesty, civility and competence in public service.

After voters elected President Trump a second time two years ago, there was reason to doubt they had any standards at all for the behavior of elected officials. Perhaps they’ve now had enough of misogyny, enmity, xenophobia, injustice, grift, greed, cruelty, chauvinism and antipathy toward the poor.

The conventional wisdom is that the electorate voted for affordability at home and accountability in Washington. That is superficially true. Trump, his team and his cronies in the billionaire bubble aggravated both concerns. Trump promised a new Golden Age but produced instead a Gilded Age , plating his presidency in 24-karat gold and building his ballroom while families worried about the price of eggs.

CEOs and other influencers, emboldened by the prospect of pardons, lavished him with largesse for his inaugural ball and his many monuments , openly bribing him in exchange for business deals, tax cuts and relaxed regulation. Meanwhile, Trump’s economic indicator was the rising tide of the 1 percent. He couldn’t grasp what the rest of the country was complaining about.

Unfortunately, the election hasn’t awakened him. “60 Minutes” correspondent Ross Douthat interviewed him a few days after the rout. When Douthat pointed out that Trump has become $3 billion richer as president , Trump responded, “So did everyone.” Douthat told Trump that wasn’t true. Trump answered, “You should have had stock.” He might as well have said, “Let them eat cake.”

Trump does not grasp the concept of public service. He treats the job as if he were CEO of the world’s largest for-profit corporation, benefiting from an utterly passive board of directors. That’s about to change.

If the midterm elections were a morality mandate, it was not the religious variety. Secular society has a moral code, too, including respect for the rule of law and every person’s “unalienable” rights. The social contract expects civility, decency and an understanding that diversity enriches society and is inevitable when people are free to believe and behave differently. The contract requires equal opportunity and compassion for the least of us. It requires the people we elect to serve us, not themselves.

Trump and his cronies have openly violated these principles. In the process, they’ve revealed a menu for aggressive congressional oversight. It won’t be easy. By elevating Stephen Miller, Trump has put his White House on a war footing. By elevating Jim Jordan to House minority leader , congressional Republicans have sent the same signal. While Trump and his people lawyer up, the rest of the country should buckle up.

The next two years will be busy as well as contentious. Democrats will have to institute accountability reforms applicable not only to Trump but to future administrations as well. They will have to take back the congressional authorities Trump has usurped and begin restoring the critical government capabilities and services Trump has destroyed.

Congress should also keep a close eye on Trump’s physical and mental health. He’s proved morally unfit for office, but 30 mental health specialists warn that he’s also showing impaired judgment and poor impulse control. In view of his sole control over America’s nuclear weapons, the health professionals warn that Trump is a “clear and present danger to the whole world.”

Most of all, Democrats should be clear about their mandate. Again, the tsunami wasn’t the left swamping the right. It was about right swamping wrong. Trump and those who still support him in Congress will characterize Democrats’ assertion of oversight as punitive and partisan rather than principled. The majority party’s committees will have to show consistently how corruption in Washington trickles down to hurt the economy and the people.

Sadly, nearly three in four Americans view the federal government as corrupt today. The next two years should be about restoring trust. If Democrats do that, they could earn the majority for a long time to come.

William S. Becker is co-editor of and a contributor to “Democracy Unchained: How to Rebuild Government for the People,” and a contributor to “Democracy in a Hotter Time.” He previously served as a senior official in the Wisconsin Department of Justice. He is currently executive director of the Presidential Climate Action Project.

articles.title: Democrats’ majority is bigger — and far more fragile — than it looks
articles.summary: Nov. 4 was a repudiation of President Trump and the broader Republican Party, not a conversion to their opposition.
articles.body:
This past election night was the worst night Republicans have had in decades, and the best Democrats have had since 2008. As of Friday, the Associated Press’s count showed Democrats with 255 House seats won and Republicans with 169, with 11 seats left to be determined. In the Senate, the Associated Press has Democrats at 55 seats against 44 for the GOP, with one seat, Alaska, not yet counted for either side.

And yet, despite these sweeping wins, 52 percent of voters told NBC’s exit poll they hold an unfavorable view of the Democratic Party. That contradiction effectively defines the 2026 midterm elections, though it is also the one Democrats are likeliest to forget. Nov. 4 was a repudiation of President Trump and the broader Republican Party, not an embrace of their opposition.

The reason is not complicated. Trump returned to the Oval Office promising to bring down costs, and voters have decidedly concluded he’s done the opposite. About two-thirds of voters said his policies had the economy worse off, and roughly eight in 10 of them voted for Democrats. Further, roughly six in 10 blamed high prices more on Trump’s policies than on external forces, and about two-thirds of House voters said his tariffs had damaged both the national and their local economy.

To make matters worse, Republicans compounded Trump’s unpopularity with flawed candidates. About two-thirds of Texas voters said Ken Paxton (R) lacked the character for the job of U.S. Senator, while roughly six in 10 South Carolinians said Darline Graham lacked the experience .

Although the Democratic Party was able to leverage this perfect storm, resulting in what has been dubbed a blue tsunami, none of it tells us whether these voters will actually stay. For one, the 15 percent of voters unfavorable to both parties — also known as double haters — broke 62-32 for Democrats this time, after splitting evenly in 2018 and voting red in 2022. By definition, they aren’t loyal to Democrats.

Independents, about one-third of the electorate, went Democratic by 20 points — the largest margin in exit polling history. Yet, those same independents rate Democrats 42 percent favorable and 58 percent unfavorable. Additionally, 7 in 10 voters under 30 backed House Democrats after splitting evenly in 2024. Yet they were only roughly 10 percent of the electorate and were especially likely to describe their vote as a rejection of Trump.

Hispanic voters also moved, with about 6 in 10 backing the Democrat. But Democrats’ party ID edge among Latinos sits at 17 points , well below its 33-point advantage in 2018. Voters earning under $50,000, about 30 percent of the electorate, went majority Democratic after splitting evenly in 2024; roughly 6 in 10 called the cost of living crucial to their vote.

Every one of these groups moved on prices — and if prices do not come down under a blue Congress, the very reason behind why they moved disappears. The mandate is therefore narrower than the margin suggests.

About eight in 10 registered voters, majorities in both parties, want the cost of living among the next Congress’ highest priorities. Asked what they want from a Democratic Congress, 44 percent cite lowering costs for groceries, housing and utilities, whereas 22 percent said investigating the administration 21 percent said impeachment.

At the same time, voters want oversight. About seven in 10, including roughly 40 percent of Republicans, say Congress is not doing enough to check the president. But oversight should not be mistaken for retribution, especially as voters continue to struggle with the everyday, kitchen-table issues candidates promised they’d address once elected. Only 36 percent want investigations to be a top priority, and while 39 percent expect Democrats to prioritize impeachment, just 21 percent actually want them to.

Critically, accountability is not a Democratic asset by default: Democrats lead on the issue of corruption by only 8 points, 38 to 30 percent , with one-third of voters trusting neither party. Now, what Democrats are least likely to appreciate is that a victory this significant is precisely what frees them to govern from the center.

The New Democrat Coalition just inducted 40 members-elect, its largest freshman class ever, bringing it to 142 members , more than half the incoming House Democratic Caucus; the Congressional Progressive Caucus has roughly 100 . Although neither faction necessarily owns this result, the largest one is certainly not the left.

And neither is the electorate itself. Moderates were the largest ideological bloc to vote, at 41 percent. Conservatives still outnumbered liberals by single digits, but Democrats won because moderates backed them overwhelmingly, 66 percent to 32 percent . Notably, the liberal share of the electorate barely moved, shifting just two points from 23 percent in 2024 to 25 percent .

In other words, Democrats did not win by growing the left; rather, they won the middle. And it is only on loan for now.

Ultimately, that is the test for Democrats ahead of 2028. Bring prices down, hold Trump and the Republicans accountable — though not at the expense of other economic issues — and these voters may stick.

Spend the majority on impeachment and culture wars, and the double haters will undoubtedly go right back to where they were only two years ago — and in 2028, Trump will not be on the ballot for Democrats to run against.

Douglas E. Schoen and Carly Cooperman are pollsters and partners with the public opinion company Schoen Cooperman Research based in New York. They are co-authors of the book “ America: Unite or Die. ”

articles.title: California’s ‘second look’ regulations could revolutionize American prisons
articles.summary: The California regulations bring new resources and expertise to bear in determining whether someone’s sentence should be reviewed or commuted. Such a reform is long overdue and very welcome, and worthy of imitation in other states.
articles.body:
On Oct. 1, California’s Board of Parole Hearings finalized a set of regulations that put the burden on the state to look at whether the people serving long sentences really need to be in prison. They say that any incarcerated person is eligible to receive a so-called Commutation and Recall of Sentence review “after completing 25 years of continuous incarceration.”

The new regulations offer the prospect of a “second look,” even to those serving sentences of life without parole, although they do not offer parole to people whose sentences preclude it.

As the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation explains, the process outlined in the new rules provides “the courts and the governor with an expert assessment of an incarcerated person’s risk to public safety before they make any prison release decision.” Incarcerated individuals who meet certain criteria “will be automatically scheduled for review.”

In the U.S. today, governors rarely grant clemency to people serving life sentences without parole . Their reluctance stems in part from the belief that they cannot safely be returned to society. The assumption has been that we should never revisit their punishment to determine what, if anything, might have changed. However, taking a second look is a rational and data-driven approach.

As a report from the Sentencing Project notes , “Evidence suggests that most criminal careers are under 10 years, and as people age, they usually desist from crime. … A robust body of empirical literature shows that people released after decades of imprisonment, including for murder, have low recidivism rates.”

Keeping people in prison long after they have aged out of criminality is very costly. The average cost states pay per year of imprisonment is more than $33,000 per person . That cost rises as prisoners age and require medical and other services.

Recognizing these facts, in 2022, the American Bar Association called on states to adopt some kind of “‘second look” policy, allowing judicial review of sentences “at designated times to determine if they remain appropriate.”

California’s new regulations respond to that recommendation and establish a multi-step review process. A hearing officer “with expertise in assessing risk meets with the incarcerated person, reviews all relevant and reliable information, and determines whether to refer the incarcerated person for a hearing.”

They can refer someone for a hearing “if it is reasonably likely that the person will receive a recommendation for a commutation and resentencing.” After such a referral, there is another evaluation, a “Comprehensive Risk Assessment” conducted by a forensic psychologist.

That assessment focuses on the question of whether an incarcerated individual “poses a high risk of future violence.” If so, the process stops there and the inmate becomes eligible for another review in three years.

If the psychologist determines that there is little risk of future violence, a formal hearing is scheduled with the Board of Parole Hearings. But the process doesn’t end there.

If it wants to recommend a sentence reconsideration or commutation, its intended recommendation is then reviewed by the board’s legal division. Whether either is done is up to the governor or the judge who imposed the initial sentence. Both have discretion to decide what to do about the recommendation; they can simply ignore it if they so desire.

And neither commutation nor resentencing, were they to happen, would guarantee that anyone would be released from incarceration.

Nevertheless, last summer, the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation sued , claiming that the Board of Parole Hearings did not have the authority to issue the new regulations without a vote by the state legislature or California voters. The foundation argues that the courts “have already decided that the law and the facts warrant a sentence of life in prison without parole or a sentence that renders the inmate ineligible for release or parole for a period over 28 years.”

CBS News reports that the state contends the regulations “simply establish a process for preparing public safety risk assessments that can be provided to courts considering sentence recall requests or to the governor when evaluating clemency petitions.”

The court has not yet issued a decision.

The California regulations bring new resources and expertise to bear in determining whether someone’s sentence should be reviewed or commuted. Such a reform is long overdue and very welcome, and worthy of imitation in other states.

Austin Sarat is the William Nelson Cromwell Professor of Jurisprudence and Political Science at Amherst College.

articles.title: Michelle Obama earns third Grammy nomination

articles.body:
Former first lady Michelle Obama could be poised for a three-peat — and could potentially break a tie for Grammy Award wins with her husband, former President Obama — after receiving her third nomination for the audio version of one of her books.

She was named as one of the contenders in the Best Audio Book, Narration, and Storytelling Recording category, during a Grammy Awards nomination announcement on Monday. Michelle Obama’s nomination is for the audio version of her 2025 fashion and style book , “The Look.”

Other nominees in the category include actor Michael J. Fox for his memoir, “Future Boy”; the late iconic country music singer Dolly Parton for “Star of the Show: My Life on Stage”; Beatles legend Paul McCartney and Morgan Neville for “The Man on the Run”; and rapper Lil Jon for “Remix Meditation.”

A win at the 69th annual Grammy Awards ceremony in Los Angeles on Feb. 7 would put Obama ahead of the ex-president in terms of wins. The Obamas have snagged two Grammys each over the years.

Michelle Obama first won a Grammy Award in 2020 for the audiobook of her memoir, “Becoming,” and again in 2024 for “The Light We Carry.” The former president won in the Best Spoken Word Album category in both 2006 and 2008.

In 2019, the former first lady also made a surprise appearance on the Grammys stage, telling the audience, “Music shows us that all of it matters — every story within every voice. Every note within every song.”

articles.title: Mamdani disbanding controversial NYPD unit
articles.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) on Monday announced that the city has disbanded the New York City Police Department’s (NYPD) Strategic Response Group (SRG), a counterterrorism unit that has been accused of using excessive force on protesters. Mamdani, in a joint statement with Jessica Tisch, the city’s police commissioner, said this will “transform” how New York…
articles.body:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) on Monday announced that the city has disbanded the New York City Police Department ’s (NYPD) Strategic Response Group (SRG), a counterterrorism unit that has been accused of using excessive force on protesters.

Mamdani, in a joint statement with Jessica Tisch, the city’s police commissioner, said this will “transform” how New York officials respond to protests by “placing communication, de-escalation and civilian coordination at the center of our approach, while protecting New Yorkers’ constitutional right to protest.”

“SRG was tasked with both counterterrorism enforcement and protest response,” Mamdani said in a video posted to the social platform X , which also featured New York City Council member Chi Ossé.

The mayor reiterated his campaign pledge to replace the SRG with this new approach, through the first-of-its-kind, civilian-led Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division (CDDD).

The division will operate through the Mayor’s Office of Community Safety and coordinate with “a specialized dialogue team” called the First Amendment Support Team (FAST), a 30-member team of officers, as part of the NYPD’s Community Affairs Bureau to “respond to First Amendment activities.”

Mamdani said that while FAST and CDDD operate, officers will be called upon to make arrests “for those engaging in civil disobedience.” He turned to Ossé in the video and added, “We both know something about that,” referring to their previous protest activities in the city.

“There will be no long guns, tear gas, kettling or pepper spray used as crowd control tactics during First Amendment activities,” the council member said. “We’re doing all of this while keeping NYPD headcount the same.”

The joint statement makes this point and adds that the reforms will be implemented at no additional cost.

Tisch noted she believes the NYPD “must always be willing” to look at its operations and seek out ways to improve. She championed the changes as something that will make the department “stronger” and “more effective.”

The NYPD’s police union, the Police Benevolent Association of the City of New York, said “today is not a good day.”

“Mayor Mamdani is showing his true colors: he’s willing to put your safety and police officers’ safety at risk to appease his radical base,” the association said in a statement . “So the next time your life is disrupted by demonstrators who are blocking bridges and roadways or causing chaos on our streets, remember: Mayor Mamdani is on their side, not yours.”

The SRG’s response to protests in the city since its formation in 2015 has been met with heavy scrutiny. Response to the unit has led to several complaints, lawsuits and settlements over the years, with protesters during the 2020 Black Lives Matter protests in New York City accusing the SRG of militarized responses and excessive force, CNN reported .

The city’s Department of Investigation found that the SRG played a “central role” in helping the NYPD during the protests, but the department also found that excessive force was used and violated the First Amendment rights of the demonstrators, the outlet added.

articles.title: Stephen Miller’s appointment signals chaos for Trump’s final two years
articles.summary: Political analysts and lawmakers expressed concern over President Donald Trump’s decision to appoint Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff, fearing his focus on controversial immigration policies and culture wars could further polarize the nation and damage the Republican Party’s future prospects.
articles.body:
In the White House, as the saying goes, “Personnel is policy.”

That’s why America needs a time-out. We have to talk about Stephen Miller.

President Trump’s appointment of Miller as White House chief of staff signals that chaos, not governing, will define Trump’s final two years in office. Miller will push harsh immigration policies and more culture war fights as top priorities for the Trump White House.

Look at what Miller had to say after the Trump-branded Republican Party was blown out in the midterms, losing at least eight seats in the Senate and 46 in the House.

Trump has “saved the Republican Party,” he said . Then Miller doubled down by twisting reality to say that with Trump as its leader the party is “stronger, more popular and more resilient than ever before.”

Karl Rove, the Republican strategist and former adviser to President George W. Bush, wrote in The Wall Street Journal that Miller’s words might be feeding flattery to Trump or “worse … he and the president actually believe it.”

Other Republicans are similarly warning of the danger in Miller’s appointment.

“He’s not liked out here in the Midwest by people, they don’t like his tone,” Rep. Marlin Stutzman (R-Ind.) told CNN .

Meanwhile, Democrats are slack-jawed at Miller’s promotion.

Here is the incoming Speaker of the House, Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), on Miller : “Stephen Miller is a stone-cold racist. His track record speaks for itself. And I’ve got zero interest in working with that kind of individual.”

The frightful consequences of Miller running the Trump White House will extend well beyond 2026.

How can 2028 Republican candidates say they are turning the page on political polarization and hatred while Trump and Miller continue writing the party’s script?

Consider the reality that voters abandoned Trump Republicans over corruption, high prices, the Iran war, the Epstein scandal, and inhumane immigration agents.

Trump and his family remain the face of the administration’s corruption, war, and Epstein scandal. But Miller’s rise rewards the heartless immigration crackdown. According to NBC News exit polls , 60 percent of voters disapproved of the way the Miller-led Immigration and Customs Enforcement is doing its job. And among those who disapproved, 87 percent voted Democratic.

An even greater share of Hispanic voters (67 percent) disapproved of ICE’s performance. The Hispanic vote took a strong swing away from Republicans in the midterms.

These numbers point away from future coalitions to expand the Republican Party. They flash red lights, warning 2028 Republican presidential and congressional candidates to run in the opposite direction.

Trump and Miller have no stake in whether the Republicans can defend or flip a single Senate seat in 2028. They want to go out in a fireball of presidential executive orders, defiance of court rulings, social media rants and defiant blind eyes to congressional subpoenas.

The damage to the Republican Party and the country will remain after Trump leaves office.

“You can forget 2028. Absolutely,” Sen. Jim Justice (R-W.Va.) told reporters about the party’s prospects of retaking the Senate . “This is such a colossal blow that it is beyond belief how colossal this is to America.”

Justice is right to be worried. Democrats have been worried about Miller for a long time.

Back in 2019, more than 100 House Democrats and over 20 Senate Democrats called for Miller’s removal . Many of them are still in Congress and about to comprise the majorities in the House and Senate.

During Trump’s first administration, I called for Miller to be fired after emails surfaced showing him circulating material associated with white nationalism and extremist anti-immigration rhetoric among reporters at right-wing outlets.

This column argued that removing Miller would help prevent the Republican Party from becoming “the angry face of one race — whites.”

“If Trump retains Miller, he will have removed the last shreds of benefit of the doubt: He is either himself a racist or someone who gives aid and comfort to avowed racists,” I wrote on this page in 2019.

I covered the White House for years and learned the power of formidable chiefs of staff. John Sununu Sr.; James Baker; Rahm Emanuel; Andrew Card and Josh Bolten were tough political players who knew how to fight. But they also showed judgment, discipline, and an appreciation for American institutions larger than themselves.

Miller is the opposite. He initially stood by ICE after its agents brutally shot Alex Pretti and Renee Good, calling them “domestic terrorists.” He has defended the abuses at ICE detention centers, including deporting people to countries they know nothing about and rough-handling people with no criminal history.

Miller’s advocacy of harsh anti-immigrant policies turned off voters who supported Trump’s earlier work to close the border.

The only way to understand Miller’s continued backing of ICE is as self-promotion, his delight in showing his extraordinary influence over the president.

Here is a simple question: Where are Republican voices demanding Trump reverse Miller’s promotion? Today, that question is more urgent than ever. That’s why Americans of all political stripes need a family time-out to talk about Miller becoming chief of staff.

The time for politics is over with the midterms in the past. It is now time to govern and time to talk about the explosive mix of Trump and Miller while we still can.

Juan Williams is senior political analyst for Fox News Channel and a prize-winning civil rights historian. He is the author of the new book “New Prize for These Eyes: The Rise of America’s Second Civil Rights Movement.”

articles.summary: Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pa.) reiterated Sunday that he is seriously considering a 2028 primary challenge against Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.), as the list of potential Democratic challengers to the senator grows. “I’m giving serious thought to running for our Senate seat in ’28,” Deluzio said during an interview with MeidasTouch. “Fetterman’s been a mess and…
articles.body:
Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pa.) reiterated Sunday that he is seriously considering a 2028 primary challenge against Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.), as the list of potential Democratic challengers to the senator grows.

“I’m giving serious thought to running for our Senate seat in ’28,” Deluzio said during an interview with MeidasTouch. “Fetterman’s been a mess and he doesn’t take the job seriously. Whatever I decide to do, that guy is not going to be the senator in ’28.”

Deluzio, who was first elected to Congress in 2022, cited “three main factors” that would determine whether he enters the race to unseat the incumbent senator.

“Does my family support this? I’ve got young kids, my wife is great, she supports me doing this. Can I win? Can I be the best senator for Pennsylvania?” he said.

The lawmaker continued, “And I think the answer to all of those is yes, then I’m in, and I’m going to win.”

His comments come less than a week after Ahmed Moor, a Palestinian American writer and businessman, became the first Democrat to launch a primary challenge against Fetterman.

Moor, a Philadelphia resident and member of the Democratic Socialists of America, announced his campaign last week, running on a progressive platform that prioritizes issues such as free healthcare and affordable housing.

Rep. Madeleine Dean (D-Pa.) also said last week she was weighing a challenge against the embattled incumbent, telling Politico she was “very disappointed in his activity as a senator and in his votes.”

Fetterman, a moderate, has faced growing criticism from fellow Democrats over his willingness to break with the party , particularly on Israel and his relationship with President Trump. His numerous appearances on Republican-friendly programming have also fueled speculation that he could switch parties.

Following a video appearance at the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention, the senator said he would not become a Republican but has warned that he would be willing to leave his party if it turns its back on Israel .

He has also seen his support among Democratic voters decline sharply, raising questions about his ability to fend off a primary challenge in 2028. Earlier this year, no member of Pennsylvania’s Democratic congressional delegation said they would back his reelection when asked.
