articles.title: Willie Geist leaving ‘Morning Joe’
articles.summary: Anchor and commentator Willie Geist is leaving MS NOW’s “Morning Joe” after nearly two decades at the table talk program. Geist will step away from the cable channel’s morning talk show to focus full time on his role anchoring “Sunday TODAY with Willie Geist” and the “Today” show. Geist was the last anchor to work for…
articles.body:
Anchor and commentator Willie Geist is leaving MS NOW’s “ Morning Joe ” after nearly two decades at the table talk program.

Geist will step away from the cable channel’s morning talk show to focus full time on his role anchoring “Sunday TODAY with Willie Geist” and the “Today” show.

Geist was the last anchor to work for both NBC News and MS NOW following last year’s spinoff of cable networks from NBCUniversal, and he has been splitting his time between “Morning Joe’s” Times Square studios and “TODAY’s” Rockefeller Center studios, the network noted.

“I am so grateful to both NBC and MSNOW for the unique opportunity to do what I love at both networks,” Geist said in a statement. “This is a bittersweet goodbye to Joe, Mika, and the place that made possible everything else in my career over the last two decades, but I am thrilled to settle in with my family at Today and dedicate all of my time to that special place.”

A presence at both MS NOW and NBC since 2012, Geist has been a major part of both networks’ coverage of politics and current events since.

He launched “Sunday TODAY with Willie Geist” in 2016, and in 2025 he began hosting a live event series featuring in-depth interviews with politicians and newsmakers.

Geist announced his move on Monday’s edition of “Morning Joe.”

articles.title: Trump ‘certainly would not mind’ Huang returning as Nvidia CEO
articles.summary: President Trump said Monday that he wouldn’t mind seeing Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO of Nvidia after he resigned last week amid extramarital affairs with several women, including one suspected of being a Chinese spy. “I would not mind. I would not mind that,” he told reporters before departing the White House for Asia. “I…
articles.body:
President Trump said Monday that he wouldn’t mind seeing Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO of Nvidia after he resigned last week amid extramarital affairs with several women, including one suspected of being a Chinese spy.

“I would not mind. I would not mind that,” he told reporters before departing the White House for Asia.

“I think he learned a big lesson,” he continued. “I guess maybe one lesson more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that.”

He also reiterated that he thinks former Apple CEO Tim Cook could take over Huang’s place as CEO.

Huang resigned Thursday following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a subordinate and one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang. U.S. officials concluded Huang was giving information to Beijing.

Trump wouldn’t say whether he thought the woman was a spy.

“I don’t know that she’s a Chinese spy, and I’ve said that,” he said. “I don’t know that she’s a Chinese spy. We’ll determine that.”

He pushed back on reports that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had told him the woman was a spy.

“I haven’t heard that he said. No, I don’t know that she is a spy,” he said. “Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy. I don’t know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don’t.”

Colette Kress, executive vice president and chief financial officer of Nvidia, will take over as interim CEO.

Trump said last week that he thought Cook would be a good fit for the job.

“NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place – TIM COOK of Apple,” the president wrote in a Truth Social post Thursday.

Cook stepped down from Apple in April after leading the company for 15 years.

Trump also defended Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, saying he wouldn’t replace him after questions were raised over his handling of export controls involving Nvidia’s advanced chips.

“They have two different views. I mean, honestly, they have two different views,” Trump said.

Lutnick was facing heat for taking a softer line on Nvidia over the company’s AI chip sales to China and not putting the Singaporean firm Megaspeed on the trade entity blacklist.

The commerce secretary has agreed to testify after bipartisan calls for him to do so.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had publicly noted Commerce’s opposition to putting Megaspeed on the blacklist.

“Treasury, War, USTR [U.S. Trade Representative] and State … were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months,” Bessent said Friday on CNBC’s “ Squawk Box .”

“But Commerce has the pen. Commerce BIS [Bureau of Industry and Security] has the pen, and you will have to ask them about their internal processes,” Bessent added.

When asked if he was considering replacing Lutnick, Trump said, “No.”

He’s “done a very good job,” Trump said.

articles.title: 3 things to expect in US politics after the 2026 midterms
articles.summary: My bet is that 2026 will be remembered as a prelude, not an interlude.
articles.body:
Two weeks ago, I wrote that “The Trump era is over.” The 2026 midterm results put an exclamation point after that assertion.

Exit polls showed 54 percent strongly disapproved of Trump’s job performance. Fifty-seven percent agreed that Trump was not a strong leader; 64 percent believed Trump does not “fight for people like you;” and 58 percent said Trump did not have the mental capacity to serve as president.

Sixty-five percent thought Trump does not have the right priorities, with 63 percent saying Trump prioritizes his personal interests, not the country’s. Sixty-six percent agree Trump’s policies have worsened economic conditions in the U.S. and 63 percent declare that prices are higher because of Trump’s policies.

Given these results, what comes next? First, JD Vance will face a serious primary challenge in 2028. His clear path to the Republican nomination has been complicated as he tries to distance himself from Trump by blaming the Republican blowout on Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran.

Come next year, Vance will have at least one or more opponents that may include Govs. Ron DeSantis (R-Fla) and Brian Kemp (R-Ga.), former Govs. Nikki Haley (R-S.C.), Chris Christie (R-N.J.) and Glenn Youngkin (R-Va.) and Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas). The Republican primary will center around the differing visions of the future of the Republican Party after Trump.

Second, we are about to return to four-party politics. Back in the 1960s, political scientist James MacGregor Burns described what he saw as a four-party politics that defined his era. Today’s new four-party politics has Democrats split between moderates who were the majority-makers in 2026 and the socialists who want an even bigger government.

On the other side of the aisle, there are the remaining Trump Republicans, whose loyalty to the president is bonded by a superglue, and the Reagan Republicans looking back to traditional conservative principles.

Some believe that the divisions among Democrats will quickly emerge in the new Congress. More likely, there will be considerable party unity, because Democrats see an urgent need to triage the damage done by Trump. This includes restoring the Obamacare subsidies, rolling back the Trump tariffs, reforming and curbing the excesses of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, ending the Iran War and more.

Healthcare and tariffs will be among the first bills introduced in the new Congress. And ending the Iran War means there will be a speedy effort to defund it. Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.), the incoming chair of the House Appropriations Committee, says , “Democrats will absolutely not fund Trump’s war of choice with Iran that has increased costs on American families and made us less safe.”

Like every major party with a broad coalition, the Democratic Party has its factions. However, given the size of the Democratic majority and the need to act decisively, Democrats are likely to resist the urge for intraparty fighting.

The Republican Party is a different story. Given its diminished ranks in the House, most of the ones who are left are Trump Republicans. The new House Republican Leader , Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), represents this branch of the party.

The Senate is a different story. There, the divisions between the Trump Republicans and the Reagan Republicans are likely to grow. Those Republican senators elected in 2024 and 2026 will remain when Trump leaves office. Given the drubbing Republicans took this year, and their primal instinct for political survival, they are likely to defy Trump and while pursuing a different path forward for their party.

Third, history will repeat itself. Trump and Grover Cleveland are the only two presidents to serve non-consecutive terms in office. Like Trump in 2024, Cleveland won a narrow reelection victory in 1892. In 1894, Cleveland’s Democratic Party suffered a landslide defeat. That year, Republicans won control of both houses of Congress, gaining 110 House seats and added four new senators to their ranks. In 1896 , the Republican Party won a landslide victory for William McKinley that began a 36-year reign of presidential dominance.

Midterm elections are either a prelude to what is to come, or an interesting interlude. Given the 2026 Democratic sweep, the odds of a realigning election favoring the Democrats has risen. My bet is that 2026 will be remembered as a prelude, not an interlude.

Whatever the political future has in store, the Trump era is over. Writing in The New York Review of Books, Fintan O’Toole observes that “the vultures are circling the Trump presidency, and the warm breeze of rotting grandeur is blowing through Washington. This is the autumn of the pungent patriarch.”

John Kenneth White is a professor emeritus at The Catholic University of America who writes on Substack . His latest book, coauthored with Matthew R. Kerbel, is titled “ Democracy on the Edge: The Trump Elections and the Future of American Politics.”

articles.title: ‘No Kings’ protest song scores Grammy nomination
articles.summary: A song bearing the same name as the “No Kings” movement that has become a rallying cry at some of the nationwide protests against President Trump’s policies is nominated for a Grammy Award. “No Kings,” by Jesse Welles and featuring Joan Baez, was among the nominees in the Best American Roots Performance category, the Grammys…
articles.body:
A song bearing the same name as the “No Kings” movement that has become a rallying cry at some of the nationwide protests against President Trump’s policies is nominated for a Grammy Award.

“No Kings,” by Jesse Welles and featuring Joan Baez, was among the nominees in the Best American Roots Performance category, the Grammys announced Monday.

Some of the lyrics in the 2025 folk song include: “No lies, no bullets. No bombs and no need for kings. No kings.”

Welles sings in another line: “No more dyin’ for the causes no one asked for, no one needs.”

Last year, 85-year-old Baez told Agence France-Presse of the song, “What’s needed is an anthem, something that everybody can sing.”

“They don’t have to worry about all the verses. Just sing the ‘No Kings, no Kings, no Kings’ part,” Baez said.

Thousands of “No Kings” protests have been held across the country this year. In March, organizers with the No Kings Coalition said demonstrators were protesting the U.S. military operation in Iran, as well as Trump’s economic agenda and his administration’s immigration crackdown.

Other nominees in the Best American Roots Performance category include: Brandi Carlile’s “You Without Me,” Sara Bareilles for “Still Crying,” Chuck Leah’s “Coyote” and Mavis Staples for “Human Mind.”

The 69 th annual Grammy Awards air on ABC on Feb. 7.

articles.title: Top Democrat accuses Commerce Department of failing to stop China from acquiring advanced chips
articles.summary: Sen. In a letter sent Sunday, Cantwell, the top Democrat on the Senate Commerce Committee, urged Lutnick to implement tougher U.S. export…
articles.body:
Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) accused Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick of putting U.S. national security at risk by failing to restrict the flow of advanced AI chips to China despite repeated warnings from federal officials .

In a letter sent Sunday, Cantwell, the top Democrat on the Senate Commerce Committee, urged Lutnick to implement tougher U.S. export controls, pointing to the department’s failure to restrict a Singapore-based company suspected of helping China obtain sensitive U.S. technology.

“America cannot maintain its leadership in AI if the agency responsible for protecting that advantage fails to enforce its own controls,” Cantwell wrote.

The letter comes as Lutnick, who is preparing to travel to China with President Trump later this week for the APEC summit, received criticism from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent over his department’s handling of Megaspeed International.

Megaspeed came under scrutiny following explosive reports of an extramarital affair between Alice Huang, a former executive at the company whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of being a Chinese spy, and former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

“Despite these warnings, the Department of Commerce delayed action on repeated national security warnings, putting America’s technological advantage in AI at risk,” Cantwell wrote.

Bessent said Friday that the Treasury Department, State Department, Department of Defense and the U.S. Trade Representative had supported blacklisting Megaspeed for months, but the Commerce Department had resisted the effort.

“Commerce has the pen, and you will have to ask them about their internal processes,” Bessent said during an interview with CNBC. “My deputy has been pushing this for months.”

Cantwell argued that after Commerce suspended its own investigation into Megaspeed left the company free to continue obtaining advanced AI chips.

The Washington Democrat also questioned whether financial interests were influencing the department’s decisions, pointing to reports that Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial services firm led by Lutnick for decades and now controlled by his sons, held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination.

“America’s national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge,” Cantwell wrote.

The Hill has reached out to the Commerce Department for comment.

articles.title: Thomas casts doubt on gun bans in ‘sensitive places’
articles.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday turned away a challenge to Maryland’s ban on carrying firearms in “sensitive places” such as mass transit sites and state parks, but Justice Clarence Thomas said his colleagues should take up the issue in a future case. “I harbor serious doubts that our Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation supports many…
articles.body:
The Supreme Court on Monday turned away a challenge to Maryland’s ban on carrying firearms in “ sensitive places ” such as mass transit sites and state parks, but Justice Clarence Thomas said his colleagues should take up the issue in a future case.

“I harbor serious doubts that our Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation supports many of these sweeping restrictions,” Thomas wrote. “In an appropriate case, this Court should consider whether particular sensitive-place laws are consistent with the right to public carry.”

Still, Thomas voted with his colleagues to not get involved, at least for now. The justice noted that each restricted location in Maryland raises distinct issues, and the underlying lawsuit challenged them too broadly.

Thomas signaled he’d vote to take up a future challenge that is “narrowly focused.”

The court’s longest-serving conservative, Thomas wrote the 2022 majority opinion requiring that gun control measures be consistent with the nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation to survive the Second Amendment.

That test has led courts to strike down a flurry of gun restrictions passed by blue states and localities in the years since. Next month, the court will hear arguments on whether AR-15 bans passed in the Chicago area and Connecticut can proceed.

Maryland, like many other states, restricts carrying a firearm in areas it deems “sensitive places.”

The Supreme Court’s conservative majority has suggested that some places — like those at schools and government buildings — have a long-standing tradition of firearm restrictions and may be permissible. But Thomas insinuated that some states are seizing on the exception to reach too far.

Maryland’s restrictions apply to mass transit facilities, casinos, places that sell alcohol, state parks, healthcare facilities and more.

“And, their cumulative effect is to prohibit firearms wherever people gather for eating, drinking, recreation, amusement, and free speech—an affront to the right of ‘law-abiding citizens,’” Thomas wrote.

articles.body:
Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio) on Sunday laid out his requirements for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) to earn his vote for House Speaker next year.

Jeffries will face a closed-door vote on the Speakership among his members this week, before a public vote for the Speaker on the House floor in January on the new Congress’s first day. Given the size of the Democratic midterm victories, he’s expected to win the Speakership.

But that doesn’t mean he won’t see some Democrats vote for other candidates.

“First of all, there was no mention in the Speaker’s letter about corruption, about ending Citizens United,” Leonard told CNN’s Manu Raju Sunday on “Inside Politics,” referencing a recent letter from Jeffries on his bid for the speakership.

“The leader knows himself, he said in an interview back in August, that the fundamental — there’s only two ways to end Citizens United and get the money out of our politics.

“Number one, reform the Supreme Court. Or number two, amend the Constitution. We need a 28th Amendment in 2028 to get this done — get the money out of our politics. If we can’t do that, we will never be able to deliver on healthcare reform. We will never be able to deliver on childcare,” he continued.

Leonard later said that another one of his requirements was to halt American aid for Israel, stating that it was his “position based on our nation’s laws and based on the conduct of the Netanyahu regime in Gaza.”

Democrats locked down the House and Senate in this year’s midterm elections, notably winning in areas where the party has struggled. Their victories mean Jeffries can lose dozens of members and still win the Speakership.

A change.org petition pressing for progressive Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.) to be named the next Speaker had hit more than 110,000 signatures on Monday morning.

The petition was released in early November and was created by the Coalition for Speaker Ayanna Pressley, “progressive activists from across the country dedicated to electing” the Massachusetts Democrat to lead the lower chamber.

In a statement, the coalition said Pressley “represents a beacon of hope and integrity in a tumultuous political landscape.”

articles.title: Four Cs for Democrats and democracy
articles.summary: Americans are disgusted by the corruption and chaos that define the Trump era, and the ways it is costing their families and communities.
articles.body:
Democratic congressional leaders are thinking strategically about the opportunity and responsibility that voters gave them on election day. That’s important because the Trump White House and its corrupt Justice Department will do everything in their power to stonewall, resist and undermine congressional oversight of administration wrongdoing.

The elevation of Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff , the authoritarian scheming of Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought and attempts by Attorney General Todd Blanche and other Justice Department officials to bully and threaten members of Congress all make it clear that the administration will continue to circumvent and defy the rule of law.

In addition, House Republicans’ selection of Trump crony Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) as their new leader signals that most of them still see their job as doing Trump’s bidding and protecting the president from any form of accountability — even after voters resoundingly repudiated what Trump and MAGA Republicans have done to the country.

That makes reported plans by democratic leaders to investigate and expose the three Cs — cost, chaos and corruption — of the Trump administration vital. The election results and exit polling make it clear that Americans are disgusted by the corruption and chaos that define the Trump era, and the ways it is costing their families and communities.

Using congressional oversight authority and the power of media and social media to expose the rot, root it out and repair the damage will keep Americans engaged in the long project of rebuilding that got started at the ballot box.

To the three Cs being discussed, I would respectfully add a fourth: cruelty.

The brutality of Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations in Minneapolis and other cities provoked a powerful community-based resistance movement of people rallying to defend their neighbors and communities from militarized onslaught. Americans were rightly outraged by government agents’ unjustified killing of activists and the lack of accountability for the killers. The public response demonstrated both the necessity and possibility of resisting an increasingly authoritarian regime.

That resistance is still needed. The continued abduction and disappearance of law-abiding and hard-working people is a daily reminder of the gross dishonesty of the administration’s claim to be focused on getting violent criminals — the “ worst of the worst ” — off our streets.

The outright sadism of Miller’s mass deportation campaign, and congressional Republicans’ repeated willingness to hand over virtually unlimited amounts of money to sustain it, turned Americans strongly against the administration. They certainly contributed to a massive loss of support among Latino voters, who gave Trump significant support in 2024 and abandoned the Republicans in huge numbers this year.

Another form of highly visible cruelty — massive ad spending targeting transgender people and their allies with vicious smears and outright lies — only highlighted the cynicism of MAGA leaders seeking to inflame fear and bigotry as a distraction from the hardship their policies have caused millions of American families. Voters saw right through it.

I believe that the cruelty combined with the brazen corruption of Trump and his family and favored insiders — unchallenged by Republican leaders — seriously undermined efforts by Trump’s right-wing Christian supporters to portray Trump as God’s anointed and to mobilize turnout.

It wasn’t a good look for MAGA religious leaders to tell supporters it was their religious duty to obey the corrupt Donald Trump and vote for the corrupt Ken Paxton, especially while at the same time smearing the faith of seminarian and state legislator James Talarico (D), who appealed to widely shared religious values of empathy, compassion, kindness to strangers and love for neighbors.

It was a tough sell. And now those same shameless religious-right leaders must contend with a growing crop of progressive leaders who authentically and enthusiastically speak about the way their faith grounds their commitment to policies that reflect compassion and fairness.

As the shrinking Republican caucus rallies around their dishonest and dishonorable president, Democrats must keep faith with voters through both truth-telling oversight and proactive legislation. Reversing MAGA policies that inflict cruelty and harm on families and communities is essential. So is holding people accountable for that cruelty and harm. Bring it on!

Svante Myrick is president of People For the American Way .

articles.title: As goes Texas: Attorneys general will spearhead abortion rights
articles.summary: A recent commitment from Texas Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson foreshadows how this sea change will affect how abortion care is delivered across the country, even in states with strict bans.
articles.body:
Abortion is always an election issue, and the 2026 midterms were no exception. Sweeping new majorities of elected officials supportive of abortion rights will join Congress, state legislatures and governors’ mansions. But down-ballot victories will also affect abortion access in some of the biggest ways since Roe v. Wade was overturned nearly five years ago .

A recent commitment from Texas Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson (D) foreshadows how this sea change will affect how abortion care is delivered across the country, even in states with strict bans.

Voters are angry about the economy, about the Iran war, and about shrinking access to health care — including abortion. Johnson understands the assignment. Within 24 hours of winning his election, he announced in an interview with the Texas Tribune that he will not continue his predecessor’s practice of suing providers in other states for sending abortion medications to Texans, stating “I can honor other states’ shield laws.”

Abortion shield laws , in effect in 23 states plus the District of Columbia, create a legal protective zone around providers, patients traveling for care, and their supporters against out-of-state anti-abortion extremists who would otherwise weaponize the legal system against them. Eight of these states’ laws explicitly protect providers of telehealth abortion services. This means they can ship abortion medications to Texas and other states that have banned abortion, knowing that officials in their home state will refuse to cooperate with a hostile state’s investigation, take away their medical licenses, process a civil judgments against them, or extradite them if they are criminally charged in the other state.

In practice, shield laws have softened the blow of losing Roe v. Wade. In July 2026, the most recent month that data is available, Guttmacher research shows an estimated 9,960 abortions were provided via telehealth by shield law providers to the 13 states with total abortion bans — 4,840 of them by Texans . The data are clear: shield law provisions have greatly improved Texans’ ability to access abortion without leaving their home state.

Of course, the story doesn’t stop there. Politicians in states that have banned abortion have continued legal and political attempts to extend their state’s laws beyond their borders; in fact, exiting Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has done just that .

That’s what makes Johnson’s promise so powerful. More attorneys general-elect should follow suit.

Although no case against a shielded provider has been successful, fear of prosecution or financial ruin serves as a deterrent for providers who may otherwise choose to offer this care. And while travelling from a hostile state to one that is protective of abortion rights remains a critical option for patients, interstate travel is expensive and can be logistically complicated, especially for those up against a running clock or choosing between paying a bill and paying for a bus ticket.

Tens of thousands of Texans, however, still travel for abortions. In 2025, almost 23,000 Texans obtained abortions in other states, most often in New Mexico and Kansas. Many traveled hundreds of miles farther to Colorado, California, Illinois and even as far as New York.

Texans deserve to make decisions about their health care needs, including abortion, without fear of being criminalized. So does everyone else. More states should pass shield laws and more governors should issue shield executive orders.

Some states, like Arizona and Pennsylvania , have shield-law executive orders that are ripe for conversion into more enduring statutory protections, now that Democrats have taken full control of both states’ legislatures in the midterm elections.

Governors play a role too, even in states where repealing draconian bans isn’t a realistic possibility next year. Governors typically appoint members of boards of health, powerful bodies that do everything from issue practice standards and guidance to discipline licensed providers, as well as oversee influential departments of health.

All of these officials potentially play a role in how abortion bans are interpreted and enforced, and they have a responsibility to allocate limited state resources responsibly. Refusing to sue shield providers and dropping frivolous and punitive investigations against them does just that.

Shield laws are working. The resilience of abortion patients, providers and helpers — including lawmakers who believe in bodily autonomy and personal health care decisions — have helped patients get the care they need, even in the face of relentless legal and political attacks from anti-abortion politicians at every level of government.

But in order to maintain this critical lifeline, we need stronger laws and providers who feel secure stepping up to deliver this care to patients. Assurances like those from Johnson are a step in the right direction and should serve as a clarion call to elected officials everywhere to use the full force of their office to protect abortion access.

Amanda Allen is executive director at Abortion Coalition for Telemedicine . Kelly Baden is vice president for public policy at the Guttmacher Institute .

articles.body:
Robert Pattinson will be the next actor to step into the iconic role of James Bond.

The “Twilight” and “Batman” star landed the part of 007 in the next iteration of the long-running film franchise, Amazon MGM Studios announced Monday.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement.

“To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement,” the 40-year-old British actor said.

Denis Villeneuve is poised to direct the forthcoming Bond film. A title and release date for the movie have not yet been announced.

“I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin,” Villeneuve said.

Pattinson joins a star-studded list of performers who have sported Bond’s signature tux, including Sean Connery, Daniel Craig, Roger Moore, Pierce Brosnan, Timothy Dalton and George Lazenby.

The announcement that Pattinson would take the reins as Bond comes months after the White House floated another potential candidate to play the leading man in the movies: President Trump.

Responding to a May post on the social platform X about auditions beginning “to find the next James Bond,” the White House replied with a politically charged nod to the famed fictional spy.

An altered black-and-white image of Trump posted by the White House showed him dressed as Bond and holding a pistol, a la 2021’s “No Time to Die” promotional art. The image included “Make America Great Again” and the 007 logo in gold-colored text.

articles.title: Was Election Day the opening shot of a new US civil war?
articles.summary: General quarters at Justice and in congressional committees have been sounded as both ends of Pennsylvania Avenue gather for war.
articles.body:
The stunning realignment of U.S. politics wrought by the Nov. 3 elections was not a vote of confidence in the Democratic Party. It was a dramatic rejection of President Trump, his policies, personality and a MAGA dominated Republican Party.

Voters did not have a third choice. And the country still remains divided despite the election results.

Both political parties are on a collision course over Trump, affordability, the excessive costs of living, corruption and a war few Americans wanted — issues that were indelibly , if not visibly, on the ballot. How bad will the collision be? Democrats will have to make good on promises made. Could the same reasons that prevent Democrats from delivering results also be the first shots fired in the next American civil war?

The president retains the veto. Elected to resolve these pressing issues, what can a Democratic Congress do? Short of obtaining a two-thirds majority in both Houses to override a veto , the answer is nothing. Ditto for any other legislation on which there is no bipartisan agreement — an idea rapidly disappearing from the lexicon.

Ruling by edict and executive order as he will, Trump will veto legislation passed only by Democrats. Presidential power will increase in the short term. Public resentment against an increasingly broken and gridlocked government will dangerously metastasize. Because both parties demean and disrespect the other, hatred has become the new political coin of the realm. The antidote for curing hate, like cold fusion, is always years away. The Constitution will suffer.

Animus and hatred between parties and a Constitution founded on checks and balances are incompatible . For checks and balances to work, compromise and civility are mandatory. Both are missing in action.

Democrats will move to destroy Trump politically. Initially, this will not lead to impeachment. Instead, massive investigations over how the Trumps have made fortunes, making the so-called Biden crime family look like high school gangs are inevitable. Democrats will demand the release of the Epstein files and, regardless of content, use them to attack Trump and his personal shortcomings.

A prospective Democratic committee chair told Republicans to “lawyer up!” The presumptive Speaker of the House labeled Chief of Staff Stephen Miller “a malignant tumor .” The presumptive chair of the House Judiciary argued the role of investigations was a return to the rule of law, aimed at weeding out massive corruption and enrichment, particularly by those close to Trump and his family.

Trump’s guaranteed reflexive action comes from his notorious mentor , Roy Cohn. He will double and triple down while refusing to give an inch to his enemies. Democrats in this hate filled environment are enemies. Consider how Todd Blanche, Trump’s attorney general, is amassing his firepower .

Through intent or ignorance, Blanche chooses not to understand that the Department of Justice was not directly established by the Constitution, but by an act of Congress. He asserted that he is the administration’s attorney for Republicans needing counsel to prevent what he wrongly argues is the unlawful assault of Democratic investigations. General quarters at Justice and in congressional committees have been sounded as both ends of Pennsylvania Avenue gather for war.

The first battle could be fought on or about Dec. 11, when the continuing resolution temporarily funding the government expires. Unless it’s extended or a budget is approved, the government shuts down. Then, when would a budget or another continuing resolution be enacted?

No rational person wants a shutdown. But hatred trumps common sense and rationality. The chances of approving a budget in this session are probably less than successfully landing on the sun. Democrats would make impossible demands on Republicans on what and what not to fund in a continuing resolution. And because Republicans are temporarily in charge of both houses of Congress, regardless of merit, who would the public blame for a shut down?

Democrats know who will be made the target for public wrath and failed government: Trump. Understanding Trump’s personality, Democrats will attempt to provoke an aging president into becoming increasingly isolated, vindictive and the sole cause of gridlock. Trump will fight back. Meanwhile, America’s adversaries will exploit this domestic civil war to accelerate our self-destruction.

Suppose the progression of violence that began with the murder of George Floyd in Minneapolis in 2020 and exploded on Jan. 6, 2021 continues? Could an ensuing breakdown of government lead to societal breakdown?

If Nov. 3 indeed signaled the first shots of a potential civil war, under the current toxic political conditions, only Americans — not its political parties — can prevent it. But will we?

Harlan Ullman chairman of a private company and principal author of the doctrine of shock and awe. His next book, co-written with Field Marshal The Lord David Richards, former United Kingdom chief of defense and due out this Fall, is “Who Thinks Best Wins: How Decisive Strategic Thinking Will Prevent Global Chaos.”

articles.title: Trump on FAA outage: ‘I don’t take any responsibility’
articles.summary: President Trump said Monday that he doesn’t take any responsibility for the Federal Aviation Administration’s nationwide ground stop last week, instead blaming the old equipment and past administrations. “I don’t take any responsibility,” he told reporters outside the White House before departing for Asia. “They did a great job — [Transportation] Secretary [Sean] Duffy —…
articles.body:
President Trump said Monday that he doesn’t take any responsibility for the Federal Aviation Administration’s nationwide ground stop last week, instead blaming the old equipment and past administrations.

“I don’t take any responsibility,” he told reporters outside the White House before departing for Asia. “They did a great job — [Transportation] Secretary [Sean] Duffy — they acted incredibly. Everybody was safe. Nobody was hurt. No crashes. No nothing.”

“And I mean, the only responsibility should be for 40 years they should have done this,” he continued.

He said he’s been working with Congress to secure funding to fix the air traffic control systems.

“I think the one good thing that comes out of it — I’m sure Congress now will give us the money to pay,” he said.

Earlier in the gaggle, Trump was asked whether he was too focused on the various construction projects around Washington, D.C. while the systems were aging.

He defended his White House renovations and called NBC’s Yamiche Alcindor “pathetic” for questioning their importance.

“Oh, you’re so pathetic. I have a responsibility to make sure the symbol of our country is in decent shape,” he said.

He went on to say the renovations to the White House take “talent,” and said the reporter doesn’t have any.

“This is peanuts. This is called talent. Talent. You don’t have talent…you don’t know what a broken column is,” he said.

“The White House was in terrible condition. Now it’s in beautiful condition. Cost me very little money to do it,” he continued. “I spent very little time to do it. And losers like you come out and they say, ‘Why are you focused on the White House?’ Because the White House is a symbol of our country.”

The FAA issued the nationwide ground stop on Friday because of what Duffy initially called a “communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.” The outage apparently started with an overloaded router in Arkansas

The ground stop was in place for nearly four hours and affected thousands of flights, causing delays through the weekend.

In a Friday evening press briefing, Duffy called for $50 billion from Congress to overhaul the air traffic control systems.

“I want $50 billion,” he said, noting President Trump had asked for $30 billion in the past. “Let’s finish this job: new hardware, new software, new telecommunication.”

articles.title: Schumer and Jeffries had their leadership job interviews the last 2 years. They failed
articles.summary: In an opinion piece, Joslin Joseph argues that the Democratic Party needs new leadership to replace Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries while holding the Trump administration accountable for its actions.
articles.body:
When times are good, anyone can look like a great leader. When times are tough, you learn who the great leaders really are. Franklin Roosevelt may or may not have had the best policies during the Great Depression, but his leadership guided people through that disaster and the ensuing World War. Donald Trump’s first term seemed to go very well, until he had to deal with a pandemic, social unrest and more.

For the Democrats, riding high after midterm elections they found a lot of new faces that they could rally around. Conversely, they have to be looking at Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) and wondering why they didn’t show good leadership the last two years. The nail in the coffin has to be the botched impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

It would be unfair to say that Schumer and Jeffries could do much from the legislative side of things. Not having control of the House or Senate, along with having a Supreme Court that was very pro-MAGA would have handicapped anyone standing up to Trump. However, they both still failed to lead.

While all Americans seemed to wonder how much worse things would get, Schumer seemed to think that “strongly worded letters” would do the trick. Jeffries presided over a House that decided to take a stronger approach to Trump by wearing color-coordinated outfits to the State of the Union. Worse, it seemed that any senator or House member would run afoul of the Democratic establishment if they decided to stand up for their citizens.

You can also look at the lack of support for young, new Democrats that won not because of party support but in spite of not getting it. Sen.-elect Abdul Ed-Sayed (D-Mich.), Sen.-elect Scott Colom (D-Miss.) and Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa (D) won despite getting tepid, if any support. Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon overperformed in Florida despite being ignored by her own party. And plenty of establishment Democrats have to be frustrated that when it came time to throw hands, they were made to sit on theirs.

Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) was targeted by the Trump administration , Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) was detained for asking a question about Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in California, Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) has been subjected to a witch hunt , the list can go on. Meanwhile, under Schumer and Jeffries’ leadership, we watched Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) schmooze his way into Trump’s good graces, Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) pull off her best Brutus impression, and the Democrats look uneven on how we treat Jewish and Muslim voters because there was little guidance from the top.

The silver lining was that in the absence of said leadership, a lot of Democrats decided to just fight. And they did. If there is one thing Americans love, it is someone who fights. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) was once considered as problematic as El-Sayed now. She is now looking at a presidential or Senate run. Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), on his own, ran a brilliant reelection campaign. So did Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton (D-Kan.), Rep.-elect Sam Forstag (D-Mont.), Sen.-elect Josh Turek (D-Iowa) and Gov.-elect Rob Sand in Iowa, and Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia.

Now that the Democrats have shocked the world, there looks to be a light at the end of the tunnel. There are still two years left of Donald Trump, but the hope is back — for now. Now that things are on the upswing, we will need to elect new leadership to ensure that if things get tough again (and they will), we won’t wander the desert without Moses to lead us. There are a myriad of senators and representatives who have the knowledge and guts to take it to the Trump administration.

There are a lot of things to be done. Most importantly, you have to fight to get inflation down, end the Iran war, see to gas prices, come up with solutions to AI and data centers, pass immigration reform and stop ICE occupations and roundups. You have to help with trade, healthcare and affordability. You have to prepare in case the stock market does have an AI bubble.

But you also have to hold Trump and company accountable for their corruption and crimes. Crypto deals need to be investigated, pay for play with foreign governments and CEOs need to be looked into, and for God’s sake, release the Epstein files.

These next two years will be complicated and we need people who know how to handle adversity and aren’t scared to do so. They also need to trust the people who are beneath them and close to their constituents to continue to fight. We are going to have a battle royale in 2028 for a Democratic nominee and that is good. Hopefully the Democratic establishment doesn’t get in the way of that. But a good way to ensure that and the other things I have listed, you can start with new leadership at the top and replace Schumer and Jeffries.

Joslin Joseph is a recipient of the 2025 Military Reporters and Editors award for Best Commentary / Opinion. A graduate of Harvard and Ohio State, he is a Marine veteran who served in Iraq. He currently lives in Anaheim, Calif.

articles.title: Fear, fantasy, and used nuclear fuel
articles.summary: The Trump administration is exploring the creation of Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses across five states to modernize the management of used nuclear fuel through reprocessing and safer disposal alternatives.
articles.body:
Federal law still says that used nuclear fuel will be buried at Yucca Mountain in Nevada: America’s only designated site for permanent disposal. But Yucca is a zombie project, alive on paper but dead in practice — just like America’s switch to the metric system. Both are congressional commitments from a bygone era, mothballed but still on the books.

Nuclear energy, on the other hand, is very much alive and scaling up to power a clean, secure, resilient, and prosperous future.

The used fuel is still around, too, sometimes at sites where the reactor itself was dismantled years ago. It sits in “dry casks,” robust steel and concrete containers that are good for a century and probably longer. Bottled up in these containers are materials that could make far more electricity. Meanwhile the former reactor sites have been cleaned so thoroughly that federal regulators have released them for any use, including farming. Yet because the used fuel remains, the sites sit largely idle while the casks are guarded 24/7 at taxpayers’ expense.

Now the Trump administration is trying to rethink the problem. It has signed memorandums of understanding with five states to explore hosting “Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses,” which could include factories to reprocess used fuel, extracting unburned uranium and plutonium to fabricate new fuel. The campuses could also host reactors, including advanced designs capable of using a wider variety of radioactive material as fuel. The sites could also be used for safe disposal of the remaining material that can’t economically produce more energy.

The U.S. Department of Energy estimates that selected sites could provide thousands of jobs and billions of dollars in long-term economic activity , boosting the regional economy. If a site provides disposal, the incentives could include funding from the more than $50 billion in the Nuclear Waste Fund , money collected from utilities to pay for disposal, under the law that made building a repository a federal responsibility. DOE says Congress must first change the law, which still limits permanent disposal to Yucca Mountain. Nuclear waste may not have a pretty face, but it has a generous dowry, if Congress decides to use it.

Resolving this decades-long stalemate could also relieve taxpayers of bearing the costs of storing used fuel around the country, while responsibly managing the remaining nuclear waste. When the DOE failed to begin accepting waste for disposal in 1998, as its contracts with the utilities called for, the utilities sued. Court judgements and settlements now require the government to reimburse reactor operators for their extra storage costs, payments come to about $800 million a year and will only grow if the stalemate continues.

The details of a path forward aren’t clear yet. But as Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), the chair of the Environment & Public Works Committee, noted at a recent hearing, the campus idea is “a good conversation starter.”

We need the conversation. Possibly the least-understood challenge in the energy field today is nuclear waste. The people who don’t understand include “environmentalists,” taxpayers, and, alas, members of Congress. “Nuclear waste” sounds awful, but it’s easier to handle than the waste products of other forms of energy production, including carbon dioxide.

No matter the details of the solution, there are a variety of policy decisions and scientific conclusions that must be reached first, and the American Nuclear Society and others are looking into these issues already. Among the changes we need:

Make the law recognize reality. Amend the Nuclear Waste Policy Act to allow consideration of other disposal sites.

Enable the DOE to make agreements with host states and negotiate over benefits and responsibilities.

Begin moving used fuel out of the places where it is stored least efficiently, namely the clusters of casks at sites where there is no longer a reactor.

Support research on new methods to recover usable materials from used fuel, a technology that dates from the 1940s but is surely ripe for modernization.

Establish scientifically validated standards for safe, secure disposal of the material that can’t be reused.

Political missteps in the 1970s and 1980s have handicapped our efforts to establish a sensible nuclear fuel cycle — one that recovers usable material from used fuel and provides disposal pathways for what’s left. Fifty years of experience shows that policymakers erred in favoring direct disposal as a way to avoid weapons proliferation. Weapons-seekers have typically bypassed reprocessing commercial used fuel, preferring more direct and efficient routes.

In addition, the designation of Nevada as the national site for final disposal underestimated the ability of an unwilling host to fend off an unwelcome repository. Finland, Sweden and Canada show what is possible with willing hosts. Finland just licensed the world’s first repository for used nuclear fuel , Sweden is building one, and Canada has chosen a site with local support. France is making progress, too. If they can tackle the technical and policy issues, certainly so can we.

At a time when scientists and engineers are making remarkable progress in fielding a new generation of clean, safe, secure nuclear power plants, it’s time to solve the used nuclear fuel issue as well.

Mark Peters is president and CEO of the MITRE Corporation.

It’s Monday. And while there’s plenty of political news we’ll get to, we can’t ignore Robert Pattinson being named the next James Bond . Between “The Odyssey,” “Primetime” and now getting cast as 007, it’s been quite the year for R-Pattz.

Programming note : Hello! We are Steff Danielle Thomas and Elliott Davis filling in for Cate. Please send your tips, comments and story ideas to sthomas@thehill.com and edavis@thehill.com .

The Associated Press | Alex Brandon and Chiang Ying-ying

President Trump , ahead of a much-anticipated trip to Asia, said Monday he “would not mind” ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang returning to his role just days after the tech titan resigned amid multiple scandals.

The president is hardly alone: More than 170,000 people, including tech billionaire Elon Musk , signed an open letter calling for Nvidia’s board of directors to reinstate Huang “while an independent investigation establishes the facts.”

The calls mark a stunning turn of events since Huang exited the CEO chair on Thursday. His resignation was spurred by several extramarital affair scandals, including one involving a woman who U.S. officials concluded was passing information to China.

Nvidia’s board launched an investigation into the matter on Nov. 8, when Huang admitted to the affair. But he resigned just days later, after The New York Times reported Huang also had an affair with a subordinate at Nvidia.

Huang himself is discussing an attempted comeback with his allies, Financial Times reported Sunday. The move comes after CNN reported last week that the U.S. intelligence community is still working to understand the relationship between Alice Huang , who reportedly had the first documented affair with the former CEO, and the Chinese government.

Regardless of what happens next, the drama has already threatened to cast a dark cloud over Trump’s trip this week to the Philippines and China, where he is expected to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping . The Hill’s Mallory Wilson and Laura Kelly have more here .

After the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued an hours-long ground- stop order on Friday, the person (or group) who deserves the largest piece of the blame pie for the outage depends on who is asked.

Trump on Monday said he doesn’t “take any responsibility” for the outage, which forced airlines to delay or cancel thousands of flights and threw air travel into disarray for days.

Government officials have initially identified old equipment as the reason for the failure and have requested additional funding to modernize air traffic control systems. But Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a Sunday interview on NBC News’s “Meet the Press” that he cannot cancel a contract with L3Harris, the firm behind the outage, noting it owns “the network.”

Duffy, meanwhile, appeared to place blame on Congress, saying that congressional funding would have enabled the FAA to transition from antiquated old copper wiring to modern fiber. But Democratic lawmakers questioned why the Transportation Department had spent only a fraction of the money already congressionally allocated.

The fight for Senate Democratic leadership is intensifying, with Sen. Chris Van Hollen (Md.) ramping up his challenge to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) ahead of the party’s leadership elections — after several lawmakers argued for a change at the top.

Van Hollen spent Sunday making his case, pushing back on suggestions that his bid is a long shot and questioning Schumer’s grip on the caucus.

Where things stand: Van Hollen dismissed doubts about his chances as “a bunch of nonsense,” telling Fox News on Sunday that he already has more than a dozen senators in his corner.

He later suggested Schumer’s team was overstating its support , telling CNN that some senators counted as backing the incumbent have privately committed to voting for him instead.

The Maryland Democrat has also criticized Schumer’s involvement in Democratic primaries, accusing the longtime leader of working with outside interests to defeat candidates who ultimately won their races.

What’s next: Schumer’s allies remain confident , predicting he’ll secure more than 40 votes. Some have also floated moving up the leadership election to settle the contest sooner.

The vote is currently scheduled for Dec. 1, though it could come as early as this week.

The increasingly public fight comes as Democrats prepare to take control of the Senate following their sweeping midterm victories.

Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) warned over the weekend that electing Van Hollen would be “troubling” because of his criticism of Israel.

But Fetterman has his own political challenges brewing.

Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pa.) is considering a 2028 Senate bid, Rep. Madeleine Dean (D-Pa.) has expressed interest and progressive activist Ahmed Moor has already launched a campaign.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is making good on a campaign promise to disband the New York Police Department’s (NYPD) controversial Strategic Response Group.

The unit, created in 2015, has faced years of criticism over its handling of protests, despite also being tasked with counterterrorism operations.

Under the overhaul , those responsibilities would be split into two teams — the Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division and the First Amendment Support Team — to help manage demonstrations. The counterterrorism duties would then shift to the NYPD’s Intelligence and Counterterrorism Bureau.

The plan also proposes new restrictions on crowd-control tactics, including limiting the use of tear gas, according to a joint statement from Mamdani and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch .

articles.title: 73 senators moved permitting reform forward. Now finish it.
articles.summary: The Senate cleared a major procedural hurdle for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, moving the long-negotiated permitting reform bill closer to passage before the end of the current Congress.
articles.body:
Last Monday, dozens of Citizens’ Climate Lobby volunteers spread across the U.S. Capitol complex in the hours before the Senate’s first vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. That evening, 73 senators voted to clear a key procedural hurdle that allows the bill to move forward for consideration.

We were glad to see it. The procedural motion, known as cloture, sets up the bill for consideration, and some senators voted yes expecting additional adjustments will be made before the final vote. There’s work to do, but the momentum is real, with the Senate expected to stay in session to keep working on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. Senators should use that time to finalize and pass it, and the House should follow suit before the 119th Congress ends on Jan. 3.

Our current permitting system is holding back clean energy and driving costs up. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act fixes that. It’s a real bipartisan compromise and a deal like this is unlikely to come together in the next Congress.

Waiting has a cost too. The permitting system we have now helped bring us climate change and puts wind, solar, and transmission projects in purgatory.

Look at what that has meant in practice. SunZia, a wind and transmission line project large enough to power about 1 million homes in New Mexico, began permitting in 2008 and just finished this year.

Cape Wind in Massachusetts, which would have been the country’s very first offshore wind farm, went through 17 different agencies and 30 separate lawsuits over the course of 15 years before it was canceled.

Then there’s Esmeralda 7 in Nevada, a solar and storage project designed to power approximately 2 million homes. Its environmental review was canceled while the project was being evaluated. Developers were told to start over and segment pieces of the project out for individual permits. None of them have moved forward.

Every clean energy project that gets put on hold means worsening climate impacts, dirtier air, fossil fuel plants that keep running in frontline communities, more threats to biodiversity, higher energy bills, and more blackouts and brownouts.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act changes all of that.

Permitting agencies get firm deadlines for reviews and permitting decisions. No longer will they be able to sit on a permit or yank permits from projects they simply don’t favor. It also makes data centers pay their fair share of grid costs and lets states set data center rates that protect households. Finally, the bill gives federal authority to approve the big interstate power lines that carry clean electricity to where people use it.

The payoff will show up in reduced emissions and lower energy costs for households across the country. Resources for the Future estimates the bill cuts power-sector emissions by about 2 billion tons through 2041 and grows total American transmission capacity by 30 percent. The Center for Climate and Energy Solutions also found that pushing these reforms back to 2030 would forfeit roughly $55 billion in electricity system savings and 800 million metric tons of emission cuts through 2040.

None of these provisions made it into the bill without thoughtful consideration, negotiation, and input from a broad array of stakeholders. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is the product of nearly two years of work and its sponsors Sens. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Mike Lee (R-Utah), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), and Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) deserve an awful lot of credit for building a consensus.

Nobody got everything they wanted in the bill and that’s the point. When concerns came up, the sponsors listened and made changes before Monday’s vote. That’s how a comprehensive permitting reform bill earns 73 bipartisan votes and why the bill has support from organizations across climate advocacy, organized labor and the clean energy industry.

This kind of agreement is rare and it likely won’t keep if we squander this moment. In January, a new Congress arrives with a new majority, new committee leaders, and new members of Congress. Permitting policy can’t pass on a party-line reconciliation bill, so even in the next Congress, any permitting reform will need support from both parties. Holding out for a different deal in 2027 requires us to bet on a bill that probably won’t come, while clean energy projects keep waiting in line and energy costs keep rising.

Citizens’ Climate Lobby volunteers know what’s at stake. Since 2023, we have held over 2,000 meetings with congressional offices on permitting reform. We did not do all that just for a procedural vote.

The Senate has done much of the heavy lifting already — finding a bipartisan deal and showing it can earn support across the aisle. Now, Congress needs to finish the job. Pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, send it to the president’s desk before the end of the year, and get clean energy built.

Ricky Bradley is executive director of Citizens’ Climate Lobby, a nonpartisan grassroots climate advocacy organization.
